usd3-3jane.title: Senior Credit Is Still Credit
usd3-3jane.text: USD3 packages 3Jane's senior credit tranche into an ERC-4626 share: USDC enters, idle cash waits in Aave, and the rest finances fintech receivables and crypto credit lines. Its NAV can rise above a dollar because interest accrues into the share price, so the familiar ticker is doing fund accounting rather than promising a fixed $1 quote. sUSD3 absorbs losses first, but that protection is only as thick as the junior tranche; recoveries from an impaired off-chain borrower can take months or years. Pharos can see the live split between liquid waUSDC and deployed credit, plus the amount immediately withdrawable, which is more useful than calling the whole balance USDC-backed. The senior seat is safer than the junior one, not the same thing as cash.

kusd-kerne.title: Genesis Beta, USDC-Backed Today
kusd-kerne.text: kUSD is Kerne Protocol's Base-native synthetic dollar, live at genesis scale but still pre-active in Pharos because the runtime price path is not ready. DefiLlama now indexes Kerne USD supply as stablecoin id 402, but the row reports price=null and CoinGecko does not yet resolve a Kerne USD coin, so Pharos keeps it on the upcoming tracker rather than the active dashboard. Current backing is simple: combined USDC reserves in the mint and redeem Peg Stability Module contracts cover outstanding kUSD slightly above 1:1. The more ambitious delta-neutral design, with a WETH vault and Hyperliquid short hedge, is documented as degraded and excluded from reserves pending a v2 redeploy. Admin authority sits with a 2-of-3 Gnosis Safe, and Kerne publishes hourly signed proof-of-reserves data at kerne.fi/verify.

usdt-tether.title: Treasury-Heavy Dollar Base
usdt-tether.text: USDT's B-grade profile is not a peg indictment; Pharos still sees an A+ peg record, while liquidity and especially decentralization do the dragging. Tether's Q1 2026 attestation shows $191.77B of assets against $183.54B of liabilities, led by about $141B of direct and indirect U.S. Treasury-bill exposure, with gold, Bitcoin, and an excess reserve buffer making the balance sheet less boring than its dollar promise. USDT0 extends the franchise across another wave of chains through lock-and-mint rails, useful for distribution and another reminder that omnichain convenience is not the same thing as issuer decentralization. The redemption floor is real for eligible Tether customers, but it remains governed by Tether's terms, discretion, and quarterly BDO Italia attestation cadence rather than continuous bank-style disclosure. July put both faces of the franchise on display in one week: when OFAC attached 131 TRON addresses to its ISIS-K designation, Tether froze every one of them within hours — sanction-machine reflexes no bank can match — while in Europe, MiCA's transitional period closed with USDT off licensed venues entirely and its regulated-market liquidity there down by more than two-thirds. On-chain supply authority is still concentrated around Tether-controlled mint infrastructure, and the 2019 accidental 5B USDT mint remains the canonical lesson in why the biggest stablecoin can be operationally serious and structurally centralized at the same time.

usdc-circle.title: The Institutional Default
usdc-circle.text: USDC is crypto's compliance-first reserve currency: cash and cash equivalents sit in the Circle Reserve Fund, managed by BlackRock and custodied at BNY Mellon, while monthly Deloitte examinations reconcile assets and liabilities. Its on-chain liquidity is unusually distributed, so a dollar that exits one venue does not have to leave the market altogether. The SVB weekend remains the historical reminder that banking access can still interrupt an otherwise conservative reserve stack. The ordinary weakness is the point of centralization: direct {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} runs through Circle, and Circle can control the token. USDC is intentionally boring infrastructure, provided the gatekeeper and its bank-and-fund chain remain boring too.

dai-makerdao.title: The OG Decentralized Dollar
dai-makerdao.text: DAI is MakerDAO's decentralized USD stablecoin; CDP-minted but now mostly backed by Treasuries and USDC via the PSM. DAI is the stablecoin that proved crypto could create a dollar without a bank account, and seven years later it still earns the highest decentralization grade in the top ten — an A that reflects genuine DAO governance rather than a multisig cosplaying as one. The reserve composition has drifted far from crypto-purist origins: 40% U.S. {{term:treasury}}Treasuries{{/term}}, 33% USDC through the {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}}, with only a quarter in crypto collateral, making DAI functionally a hybrid fiat-crypto dollar. More depeg events on record than any other major stablecoin sounds alarming until you notice the peg score still sits in the high nineties, and the {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop — atomic PSM access at zero fee — scores higher than almost everything else on the dashboard. Now overshadowed by its own rebrand as USDS, DAI occupies a strange position: the philosophical North Star of decentralized money, increasingly backed by the centralized assets it was designed to replace. {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} vaults remain the original minting path.

frax-frax.title: The Identity Crisis
frax-frax.text: FRAX abandoned its {{term:algorithmic}}fractional-algorithmic{{/term}} origins to become a tokenized {{term:treasury}}T-bill{{/term}} basket — clean reserves, scarred history, awkward middle ground. The current balance sheet leans on Frax-owned liquidity, WisdomTree WTGXX, Superstate USTB, BlackRock BUIDL, and a smaller Ethena/Convex strategy sleeve, which is a long way from the reflexive coin that once made the brand famous. The reserve reads like an institutional allocation, yet the report card still treats the dependency stack and old peg scars as unresolved baggage rather than ancient history. FRAX sits in the uncomfortable middle: too decentralized-dependent for institutional comfort, too TradFi-backed for DeFi purists. A wide spread of DEX pools sounds impressive until concentration math and merely passable liquidity undercut it. The yield via Vesper lending barely compensates for that ambiguity — you are not being paid much to hold a stablecoin still arguing with its own origin story.

tusd-trueusd.title: Transparency in Name Only
tusd-trueusd.text: TrueUSD's reserves tell the whole story: 99% parked in opaque First Digital Trust fund investments rated very-high risk, 1% in actual cash, all under a British Virgin Islands domicile with no meaningful regulator — the exact opposite of what the brand once promised. The Chainlink Proof of Reserve feed provides an {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} that reserves exist but says nothing about what those reserves actually are, which is like a fire alarm that confirms the building is there but not whether it's burning, and the underlying {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} chain stays just as opaque. Supply has been effectively frozen for weeks with little movement, an unusual pattern that suggests either minting is paused or demand has fully calcified, and the {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} path through Techteryx offers little additional clarity. The peg itself holds tight, but dozens of past depeg blips and a C- report card describe a token that survives on institutional inertia rather than active confidence — still traded, still liquid enough on its DEX pools, but no longer trusted the way its name demands.

lusd-liquity.title: The Immutable Benchmark
lusd-liquity.text: LUSD remains the philosophical standard for decentralized stablecoins: ETH-only collateral, immutable contracts, no admin keys, no governance, no upstream dependencies — which is what earns it an A overall and a near-perfect read on every structural axis. The permissionless {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop is the load-bearing piece, providing a hard floor at $1 by letting anyone swap LUSD for $1 of ETH from the riskiest Trove in exchange for 50 bps. The hundreds of recorded sub-peg blips reveal the trade-off of purity rather than weakness: ETH-only backing at 110% minimum pushes borrowers to hold safety margins, producing persistent above-peg drift, and every ETH crash tests the Stability Pool's absorption capacity in real time. Supply keeps slowly bleeding, the fate of a v1 protocol overshadowed by its own successor BOLD, which added multi-collateral support and user-set interest rates. LUSD is increasingly a monument rather than a market participant — the stablecoin that proved decentralization works and then watched the market choose convenience anyway.

mim-abracadabra.title: The Cockroach of DeFi
mim-abracadabra.text: Battle-scarred {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} stablecoin minted against Abracadabra cauldrons; reflexive peg, no modeled {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop, and a remaining user base too stubborn or leveraged to leave. Magic Internet Money has survived multiple cauldron exploits, a treasury-manager scandal, a governance token collapse, and a long history of violent peg excursions, which makes its continued existence less a triumph than a lab result. The collateral base still reads like a museum of DeFi exotica: yvDAI dominates, WBTC is material, and smaller yvWETH/WETH cauldrons keep the wrapper risk alive. The mechanism is reflexive rather than structural — borrowers buy discounted MIM to repay debt, which only works when borrowers exist and care about their positions. June finally broke the pattern: MIM crashed through half a dollar in its worst depeg on record, Abracadabra's emergency response — rate hikes, incentive pauses, a token Curve-pool injection — failed to hold the line, and Pharos's multi-source feed now prices the token at a deep double-digit discount with the report card at F. The cockroach earned its title by surviving what killed everything else; this time the exterminator appears to be arithmetic.

usdp-paxos.title: The Regulator's Pet
usdp-paxos.text: Paxos's USDP is backed by very-low-risk reserves split across short-dated {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}}, overnight repos, and FDIC-insured cash under a KPMG-attested OCC National Trust Charter. The peg and resilience profile are the product's obvious strengths; the gap between those marks and a genuinely elite profile lives in liquidity, which remains the asset's perennial soft spot. USDP has become less a growth product than a credentialed reference implementation — Paxos's real business is white-labeling stablecoin infrastructure for PayPal, Global Dollar Network, and formerly Binance. The depeg events on record read like thin-market artifacts rather than backing failure, but thin markets are still what holders have to trade through. The current package remains one of the cleaner compliance-to-reserves stories in the small-cap tier, with zero-fee {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} as the structural floor under a token almost nobody seems eager to hold.

usdd-tron-dao-reserve.title: The Reinvention That Won't Quit
usdd-tron-dao-reserve.text: USDD has pivoted again: the reserve now shows 62.5% TRX and 1.1% sTRX as CDP collateral alongside 31.5% in Smart Allocator DeFi strategies and 4.9% USDT in PSM vaults — a return to the TRX-heavy {{term:algorithmic}}volatile-asset{{/term}} composition that defined USDD's earlier era. That is a striking backing profile for an asset that now sits at a C- overall safety grade, dragged down by an F on decentralization and the structural fact that its dollar value rests on the most volatile single asset in the TRON orbit. The peg itself behaves better than the rest of the profile deserves, and the asset rarely strays from the calm end of the stress scale, but that surface stability has been bought across hundreds of brief deviations over the years. The 95-rated {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}} backstop remains the load-bearing piece: permissionless atomic swaps with zero fees and an immediate USDT exit lane provide a redemption quality the surrounding reserve mix can't match. With Dominica jurisdiction and governance still set by fiat, USDD survives not on collateral merit but on the TRON ecosystem's captive demand and its founder's conviction that centralized control is a feature.

dola-inverse-finance.title: Scars That Built Armor
dola-inverse-finance.text: DOLA is Inverse Finance's CDP-style stablecoin minted via FiRM lending, with a USDS PSM as its peg floor. Inverse Finance's twin $24M exploits in 2022 left scars that became load-bearing, and the protocol genuinely rebuilt from near-zero credibility on the back of FiRM's fixed-rate lending markets generating organic borrower demand. But the C- grade reflects a collateral base that has quietly become anything but diversified: sUSDe now makes up roughly 89% of the backing, which is why the dependency grade sits at F and DOLA's fate is effectively chained to Ethena's synthetic dollar. The sDOLA {{term:yield-bearing}}yield{{/term}} remains the quiet attraction here, sourced from actual borrower interest rather than token emissions, and DEWS tends to hover near the cautious end of the stress scale rather than the calm one. DOLA survived exploits severe enough to end many protocols, but hundreds of brief sub-peg blips and a worst deviation that once approached total collapse remain the asterisk on every metric, and the {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}}'s USDS backstop is real but thin against that history. DOLA is minted from overcollateralized {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-style FiRM loans with {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} backstops.

sdola-inverse-finance.title: DOLA With an Exchange Rate
sdola-inverse-finance.text: sDOLA is the ERC-4626 wrapper around DOLA's savings account, which means the stablecoin risk is still DOLA and the extra product risk is the exchange-rate wrapper sitting on top. FiRM borrowing revenue is converted through the DBR-DOLA auction and compounded into a rising DOLA:sDOLA exchange rate, so the yield story is at least tied to borrower demand rather than a mystery emissions spreadsheet. The wrapper does not create new base DOLA supply, but holders still inherit DOLA's CDP collateral mix, governance scars, and any upstream stress in the parent peg. Cross-chain deployments on Base, Optimism, Arbitrum, and Berachain broaden access while keeping Ethereum as the source of truth, which is convenient until the bridge path becomes the part everyone suddenly remembers.

gusd-gemini.title: Pristine Reserves, Ghost Town Liquidity
gusd-gemini.text: GUSD is Gemini Trust's NYDFS-chartered dollar redeemable 1:1 against State Street/Western Alliance cash and short {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}} — pristine compliance, almost no users. Gemini Dollar's reserve is impeccable: 62% T-bills and 38% cash at State Street and Western Alliance Bank, NYDFS trust charter, and zero {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} fees. The problem is that nobody uses it, and that gap now drags the overall safety grade down to B- — the spotless backing simply cannot offset a market that won't trade the thing. At $44M circulating — down from a peak well above $300M — GUSD has become a regulatory trophy collecting dust, with a D liquidity grade that makes on-chain exit a theoretical exercise. Its hundreds of brief price blips are the signature of an asset so thinly traded that any flow nudges the quote, with the sharpest excursions skewing negative even as the peg recovers each time. Gemini built the compliance-first stablecoin that regulators asked for, and the market responded with a collective shrug.

alusd-alchemix.title: Time Pays Your Debt
alusd-alchemix.text: alUSD is Alchemix's self-repaying {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} stablecoin: deposit DAI, USDC, or USDT into Yearn and Aave yield strategies, borrow up to roughly 50% against it, and let the yield slowly erase your debt with no interest and no {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} risk. The mechanism remains DeFi's most patient financial product, and the Transmuter still backstops 1:1 {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} on a queue that settles over days. But the elegance has a price the report card now spells out plainly: an overall F, a peg that grades D and an active depeg in progress, because self-repaying loans strip out the debt-repayment urgency that normally generates buying pressure to defend the peg. The peg has logged over a thousand brief deviations across its history and rarely sits comfortably at the calm end of the stress scale, so holders are effectively trading away peg discipline for the no-liquidation guarantee. Liquidity is the other casualty, grading F as exit routes have thinned, and only the structurally sturdy parts of the design hold up: resilience earns a B+ on its battle-tested architecture and dependency a B, which together make this a stress-prone instrument that only makes sense if you value never being liquidated above all else.

susd-synthetix.title: Retired Below Par
susd-synthetix.text: Synthetix's sUSD is no longer the simple SNX debt-pool dollar older DeFi muscle memory remembers. The current reserve story is split across legacy SNX exposure, V3 USDC/stataUSDC collateral, ETH/LST collateral, and protocol treasury or SLP-vault activity, which is a long way of saying the peg now depends on governance executing a cleanup plan. Pharos flags the prolonged discount because this is not a theoretical stress test; the token has been living below its target while the V3 transition and basis-trade restoration plan try to rebuild demand. The mint path is governed through Synthetix admin control rather than immutable borrower autonomy, so holders are underwriting both collateral volatility and political patience. In June the roadmap ran out: governance passed SIP-423, retiring sUSD outright — the contract frozen, holders compensated at four SNX per sUSD on a year's lock and a year's vest, and Pharos no longer gets a continuous price read on what was DeFi's original synthetic dollar. Eight years of peg engineering ends not with a bang but with a conversion schedule.

ousd-origin-protocol.title: The Passive Yield Play
ousd-origin-protocol.text: Yield-bearing rebasing USDC wrapper that deploys deposits into Morpho and Curve strategies; non-opted holders subsidize opted holders, with one of the stronger permissionless redemption backstops in the yield-bearing set. Origin Dollar is fully backed by USDC routed through Morpho/Yearn vault exposure and Curve {{term:amo}}AMO{{/term}} liquidity, {{term:yield-bearing}}rebasing daily{{/term}} so balances grow without staking or locking. The clever twist is that smart contracts must explicitly opt in to receive yield, so OUSD sitting in non-opted AMM pools effectively subsidizes everyone else's returns. Permissionless atomic stablecoin {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} at a small fee provides a structural floor that many depeg blips have tested but not broken. The exotic collateral quality and wrapper governance classification reflect what OUSD actually is: a USDC yield strategy with a rebasing token wrapper, not an independent stablecoin with its own reserve management. It is a well-engineered product for the small cohort that wants DeFi yield without the DeFi homework, and the cohort remains tellingly small.

cusd-celo.title: Stablecoins All the Way Down
cusd-celo.text: USDm is Mento's oracle-priced USD stablecoin on Celo, mostly backed by other stablecoins with a CELO wildcard. Mento Dollar (USDm, formerly cUSD) is an exercise in recursive stablecoin nesting: the reserve leans on sUSDS (~44%), with USDC, USDT, and EURC slices on top, meaning the majority of USDm's backing is itself backed by other stablecoins, each with its own dependency chain and failure modes. A long tail of mostly minor depeg events and a worst drawdown past 11% are hard numbers to look past, though the C report card suggests the Mento AMM's circuit breakers have tightened since the worst of it, even if the stress gauge still flickers off the calm end from time to time. The thesis remains phone-number wallets in places like Nairobi, not DeFi composability on Ethereum. The ~14% CELO allocation is the wildcard in an otherwise stablecoin-heavy reserve: the one asset that can crater in a downturn precisely when the {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} ratio matters most, and the reserve only runs around 1.25x. {{term:redemption}}Redemption{{/term}} runs through Mento reserve swaps rather than fiat off-ramps.

eurc-circle.title: MiCA's Compliance Moat
eurc-circle.text: Circle's EURC is the regulatory standard-bearer for euro stablecoins: ACPR-licensed EMI under MiCA, {{term:attestation}}Deloitte-attested{{/term}}, 99% of reserves in deposits at systemically important European institutions, deployed natively across six chains — Ethereum, Base, Avalanche, Solana, Stellar, and World Chain. The B+ grade reflects institutional plumbing that works exactly as designed, with top-tier resilience and a DEWS reading that rarely leaves the calm end of the stress scale — though its handful of logged depeg events includes one brutal drawdown near 95% below peg, almost certainly a data artifact or thin-market episode that skews an otherwise pristine record. At several hundred million euros circulating, EURC is the largest euro stablecoin by a wide margin, yet that figure would barely register as a rounding error on USDC's balance sheet — the structural gap between dollar and euro stablecoin demand remains the defining constraint. The moat in the title stopped being theoretical on July 1, when MiCA's transitional period lapsed for good: USDT liquidity on regulated European venues has collapsed, and Circle's pair — USDC and EURC — is what remains on licensed shelves. Liquidity earns an A on the back of organic, well-distributed depth, the kind that comes from being the default euro pair on every major DEX. Institutional {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} backs 1:1 {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} via Circle Mint.

eurs-stasis.title: First Mover, Fading Advantage
eurs-stasis.text: EURS is STASIS's euro stablecoin redeemable 1:1 against EU bank balances — the original euro stablecoin, now watching better-funded rivals methodically take its market. The static file still reads respectable: Malta MFSA context, BDO Malta {{term:attestation}}attestations{{/term}}, and liquid euro balances at licensed European institutions including central-bank accounts. The live report card is far less polite, with a failing overall profile driven by the peg rather than by reserve composition. That matters because EURS is not merely carrying historical scar tissue; the dashboard has been showing active stress where a mature fiat-backed euro token should look boring. Liquidity is the one bright spot, reasonably distributed compared with other small euro coins, but distribution cannot repair a quote that keeps slipping. The verdict holds: pristine {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} and recurring attestations can keep a product alive, but they cannot make the market price it at par.

ceur-celo.title: The Other Mento Euro
ceur-celo.text: EURm is Mento's oracle-priced EUR stablecoin on Celo, sharing the Mento reserve at ~136% overcollateralization. Mento Euro (EURm, formerly CEUR) shares the same Mento reserve as Mento Dollar — 56% sUSDS, 22% EURC, 12% CELO, and smaller positions in various stablecoins and ETH — at approximately 136% {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}}, stabilized via the BiPoolManager virtual AMM with oracle-enforced EUR rates. As a crypto-backed coin, EURm inherits both the strengths (on-chain transparency, overcollateralization) and weaknesses (crypto collateral volatility, thin secondary markets) of the Mento system. Deployed on Celo (now an Ethereum L2) with real-time on-chain reserve verification, EURm exists primarily to serve Celo's vision of region-specific stablecoins for mobile payments rather than DeFi composability. In the euro stablecoin race dominated by Circle's EURC and MiCA-licensed competitors, EURm's niche is geographic rather than regulatory. {{term:redemption}}Redemption{{/term}} runs through Mento reserve swaps rather than fiat off-ramps.

fpi-frax.title: CPI on a Blockchain
fpi-frax.text: FPI is Frax's CPI-tracking stablecoin backed by FRAX reserves and {{term:amo}}AMO{{/term}}-generated yield — an inflation derivative with single-issuer dependency. Frax Price Index does not peg to a dollar — it pegs to purchasing power, with a {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} price that ratchets upward every second at the trailing 12-month CPI-U rate via Chainlink oracle. That makes it both a stablecoin and an inflation derivative, backed entirely by FRAX reserves and AMO yield, which is exactly the recursive dependency the safety grade — now down at D — punishes: FPI's collateral quality is only as good as FRAX itself, and the chain inherits every flaw upstream carries. Liquidity is the other anchor dragging it down — a failing F grade and one of the thinnest markets tracked on Pharos, spread across a handful of DEX pools with no depth to absorb a real exit. A clever idea trapped in a thin market with a single-issuer dependency chain.

uusd-youves.title: Dead Protocol Walking
uusd-youves.text: Youves's uUSD is a Tezos {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} backed by XTZ, tzBTC, USDt, and SIRS LP tokens, with a safety score of literally zero and a permanently failed peg around $0.935. uUSD has earned the only distinction worse than an F grade: a safety score of literally zero, the absolute floor of the Pharos scale, shared with almost no other tracked stablecoin. Trading at $0.935 with thousands of recorded depeg events and an 8,890-basis-point worst positive deviation, uUSD exists in a state of permanent, currently active peg failure on a Tezos ecosystem that has effectively emptied out beneath it. The collateral — 60% XTZ, 20% USDt-on-Tezos, 10% tzBTC, 10% SIRS LP tokens — still technically backs the {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}s via {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} with {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} mechanics, but zero DEX liquidity, zero pools, no backstop route, and a stress monitor pinned at the alarm end of the scale confirm there is no market mechanism left to enforce the peg. Supply has barely moved in months at $11.6M, which is not stability but rigor mortis. The uUSD story is a cautionary tale about chain risk: sound {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} mechanics are worthless when the entire ecosystem around them goes dark.

lisusd-lista.title: BNB Chain's CDP Bet
lisusd-lista.text: BNB Chain CDP backed mostly by BNB-ecosystem assets (BNB, slisBNB, BETH, BTCB) with a PSM against USDT/USDC/FDUSD; 387 depeg events on the record. Lista DAO's lisUSD transplants the MakerDAO CDP playbook to BNB Chain with a collateral mix that is 60% BNB ecosystem assets — 35% native BNB and 25% slisBNB (Lista's own LST) — plus 15% Binance-wrapped ETH and 10% BTCB, with a PSM accepting USDT, USDC, and FDUSD for peg stability. The 387 depeg events including one that cratered nearly 6,000 basis points below peg make lisUSD one of the most frequently depegged CDPs at scale, though the 85-rated PSM backstop with permissionless atomic settlement provides the structural floor. Deployed only on BSC with alt-LST collateral quality and no jurisdiction or proof of reserves disclosed, lisUSD's safety profile depends entirely on BNB's price stability and the PSM's capacity to absorb redemption pressure. Whether lisUSD can grow beyond Binance-subsidized adoption remains the central question — a CDP whose collateral and distribution both flow through a single ecosystem. The model is a standard {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} with BNB-heavy {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}}, LST-collateral {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} risk, and a permissionless atomic {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}} as the peg floor.

eure-monerium.title: SEPA Native, DeFi Adopted
eure-monerium.text: EURE is Monerium's MiCA-regulated euro e-money; SEPA-native mint and burn, mostly backed by an LVNAV fund plus bank deposits. Monerium's EURe is what happens when an Icelandic EMI license meets actual product-market fit: SEPA-to-IBAN integration that lets users move between euros and on-chain tokens without the friction that plagues most stablecoin on-ramps, backed by 70% State Street AAA-rated EUR liquidity fund and 30% bank deposits at Arion and LHV. The B grade matches EURC's safety profile despite Monerium's smaller scale, and steady double-digit monthly supply growth signals that a deployment now spanning nine chains — Ethereum and its L2s, Gnosis, Polygon, and Cosmos rails — is finding traction. DEX liquidity remains the weak point — depth still tilts toward a couple of dominant pools even as the venue count has widened, leaving EURe exposed to concentrated withdrawal risk that the underlying reserves would comfortably cover but the market might not wait for. Iceland's FSA may lack the brand cachet of France's ACPR, but the reserve structure and {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} model are functionally indistinguishable from the top tier. The 70% State Street allocation is a low-volatility {{term:money-market-fund}}money-market fund{{/term}}, and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} burns EURe and credits EUR via SEPA.

eusd-electronic-usd.title: The Boring Basket That Works
eusd-electronic-usd.text: eUSD is a Reserve Protocol RToken wrapping Compound and Aave USDC/USDT lending positions, with RSR stakers absorbing first-loss — a {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} basket that's matured into a workhorse. Electronic USD takes three of the safest yield positions in DeFi — Compound V3 USDC, Aave V3 USDC, and Compound V3 USDT in roughly equal thirds — wraps them in Reserve Protocol's permissionless basket {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} mechanism, and lets RSR stakers absorb the first-loss risk. The peg and resilience grades both sit at A+, and atomic permissionless redemption against the live basket is among the stronger exit routes in the crypto-backed category; eUSD rarely strays from the calm end of the stress scale. So why only a B- overall? The drag is structural: a D on decentralization and a C+ on dependency, because the whole thing is governed by per-RToken stakers and leans entirely on the health of Aave, Compound, and the USDC/USDT underneath — the wrapper inherits every upstream risk it's built on. The hundreds of historical depeg blips are real but largely ancient, the worst a roughly 13% gash in earlier days, while peg stability today and a three-chain deployment across Ethereum, Base, and Arbitrum suggest the mechanism has settled. Supply has been essentially flat near $23M for months, neither growing nor contracting, which is either stability or irrelevance depending on your perspective.

crvusd-curve.title: Curve's Own Medicine
crvusd-curve.text: crvUSD is Curve's {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} stablecoin with LLAMMA soft-liquidation; deep DEX liquidity, but most collateral is custodial WBTC/cbBTC. When the protocol that dominates stablecoin DEX routing launches its own stablecoin, the design had better be interesting — and LLAMMA is, replacing cliff-edge {{term:liquidation}}liquidations{{/term}} with gradual rebalancing through price bands. The report card remains solid rather than elite because the collateral story contains a structural contradiction: Bitcoin collateral running through BitGo and Coinbase introduces exactly the centralized {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} dependencies crypto-native collateral was supposed to avoid. PegKeeper pools paired with USDC, USDT, PYUSD, frxUSD, and GHO provide active peg machinery, while scrvUSD creates a yield feedback loop where stress can pull buyers back in. Curve still gives crvUSD the deepest on-chain liquidity footprint among CDP dollars, but even home-field advantage cannot fully insulate a crypto-backed stablecoin from the deleveraging cycles that govern its borrowers.

gho-aave.title: DeFi's Most Liquid Dollar
gho-aave.text: GHO is Aave's decentralized dollar minted by borrowing against any Aave V3 collateral — a diversified {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} dollar drawn from the protocol's battle-tested pools. It carries a B overall safety grade on Pharos, a grade that undersells its two best traits and fairly prices its weakest: peg behavior and liquidity both rate near the top of the scale, while reliance on Aave governance and on a handful of yield-bearing GSM facilitators keeps decentralization and dependency capped in the B range. The redemption backstop, anchored by the {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}} swap mechanism and stablecoin-backed stability modules, is about as clean as on-chain exit routes get. The hundreds of brief sub-peg blips and a worst-case deviation north of 600 bps are scars from GHO's rocky early months that the current architecture has largely healed; the peg has long since settled into the calm end of the stress scale. Liquidity is the standout — a deeply distributed DEX footprint earns the highest grade on the board, and sGHO staking layers a yield on top without leaning on exotic collateral. That dependency got a live test this spring: the Aave Chan Initiative — the delegate shop that shepherded GHO from $35 million to over half a billion — completed its exit from the DAO amid a governance rift that also saw core developer BGD Labs walk away. GHO itself kept moving regardless; the Monad deployment, its first beyond Ethereum and its L2s, drew nine figures of deposits within days. Aave proved a lending protocol can birth a credible dollar if it is willing to iterate in public; the B grade is the bill for the governance dependency that credibility still rides on.

fdusd-first-digital.title: Binance's Current Favorite
fdusd-first-digital.text: FDUSD is a BVI-issued dollar stablecoin backed by {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}} and bank deposits with IAPA {{term:attestation}}attestations{{/term}} — clean reserves, but the same custodian lineage as troubled TUSD. First Digital USD rose to prominence as Binance's preferred stablecoin after BUSD's regulatory demise, and its reserves are genuinely clean: 74% T-bills, 18% cash, and the rest in bank deposits and overnight repos — all very-low risk, attested by IAPA International and Prism. The connection to First Digital Trust — the same {{term:custody}}custodian{{/term}} whose opaque fund investments make TUSD's reserves a red flag — is the uncomfortable shared lineage, though FDUSD's own reserve composition is transparent and conventional. Deployed across six chains including Sui, TON, and Solana alongside the expected EVM networks, the distribution follows Binance's ecosystem preferences more than organic DeFi demand. FDUSD's fate remains a single-dependency story: Binance's endorsement made it, and Binance's pivot to another preferred stablecoin could unmake it just as quickly.

pyusd-paypal.title: The Respectable Waiting Room
pyusd-paypal.text: PayPal's KPMG-attested PYUSD has one of the cleanest reserve profiles tracked; the open question is whether PayPal's enormous user base will ever use it natively. The reserve composition remains almost aggressively boring: 97% {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} reverse repos, 3% cash, KPMG-{{term:attestation}}attested{{/term}}, under Paxos's OCC national trust charter. Pharos still treats the structure as high quality, but the live grade has softened from the earlier top-tier claim as liquidity and real adoption do more work in the score than brand recognition does. Multi-chain deployment, zero-fee {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}}, and Morpho yield routes make the token technically easy to defend. One adoption vector firmed up in June: Mastercard added PYUSD to its stablecoin settlement expansion, putting Paxos-issued rails into card back-office flows — B2B plumbing rather than retail spending, but real usage nonetheless. The lingering question has shifted from whether PYUSD can compete to whether PayPal's retail network will ever use it on-chain, or whether the float is mostly crypto-native capital parking in a very respectable waiting room.

gyen-gyen.title: Regulated in the Wrong Country
gyen-gyen.text: GYEN is GMO Trust's NYDFS-chartered yen stablecoin backed by FDIC cash and {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}} — pristine custody, near-zero on-chain usage, and now an orderly wind-down notice. It holds the distinction of being one of the most heavily regulated JPY stablecoins in existence, though the regulator is New York rather than Tokyo. GMO Trust's charter, monthly Network Firm {{term:attestation}}attestations{{/term}}, and very-low-risk reserve model would be impressive if the market still cared. The problem is the secondary market: thin DEX liquidity and a long depeg history make GYEN trade less like a stablecoin and more like a neglected FX derivative. The 2021 depeg litigation and 2026 wind-down notice turn the dashboard's failing profile into a verdict rather than a warning. This is pristine {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} architecture wrapped around a token whose main remaining use case is redemption before the lights go out.

usdy-ondo-finance.title: Two Billion Reasons to Notice
usdy-ondo-finance.text: Ondo's USDY carries a C+ safety grade, and the spread of its sub-scores explains the discount better than any headline figure: pristine, very-low-risk collateral on one side, a centralized governance posture and thin tradeable depth on the other. The backing is about as clean as tokenized {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} exposure gets — short-term U.S. Treasuries, iShares short Treasury ETF shares, and bank demand deposits, with daily NAV {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} from Ankura Trust — which earns USDY strong resilience and dependency marks. What drags the grade down is everything around that collateral: a failing decentralization score reflecting the BVI-domiciled, issuer-controlled structure with a multi-day {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} window, plus weak on-chain liquidity despite a footprint spanning roughly a dozen networks from Ethereum and Solana through Cosmos chains like Noble and Mantra. The peg itself stays unremarkable — no depeg events on record and nothing flagging stress — which is the point of a {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} NAV token that accrues value rather than chasing a hard dollar. USDY remains a clean way to hold American government debt for the non-U.S. investors that American regulators won't let buy it directly; the grade simply prices in that you're trusting Ondo's plumbing, not a market, to get your money back.

cadc-cad-coin.title: Canada's Lonely Loonie
cadc-cad-coin.text: CADC is a centralized, FINTRAC-registered CAD stablecoin; reserves sit in trust at a regulated Canadian institution. CADC is backed 100% by CAD and liquid securities (sub-90-day maturity) in a segregated trust, registered with FINTRAC as an MSB (C10001420) under the Loon brand, with institutional-regulated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} and self-reported reserve transparency via a Dune dashboard. Deployed across four chains including Ethereum, Polygon, Arbitrum, and Base, CADC has broader EVM reach than most local-currency stablecoins despite its modest scale. The Canadian stablecoin market remains wide open — the Bank of Canada has urged federal regulation but Parliament hasn't acted — and CADC's bet is that being the first compliant CAD stablecoin matters more than being the biggest. Whether first-mover advantage in a market waiting for regulatory clarity is a position of strength or a position of uncertainty depends on how fast Ottawa moves. {{term:redemption}}Redemption{{/term}} is 1:1 against CAD held in segregated trust.

cadd-cad-digital.title: Canada's Institutional CAD Rail
cadd-cad-digital.text: CADD is a regulated CAD stablecoin from Tetra Trust with trust-segregated reserves, awaiting usable live price and supply data. CADD launched on May 4, 2026 as a CAD-pegged stablecoin issued through Tetra Trust's regulated framework, with Alberta Treasury Board and Finance approval and trust-segregated reserves dedicated to {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}}. The token has Ethereum and Base contracts, while issuer materials list Tempo and forthcoming Solana support, positioning CADD as an institutional settlement rail rather than a retail DeFi product first. CADD remains coverage-pending because DefiLlama and CoinGecko list the asset but currently do not expose usable live price and supply data. Monthly Baker Tilly reserve {{term:attestation}}attestations{{/term}} and daily reserve-ratio disclosures provide a stronger transparency baseline than many long-tail fiat stablecoins if active market data follows. Institutional trust {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} sits under Alberta's Loan and Trust Corporations Act.

usde-ethena.title: The Basis Trade, Tokenized
usde-ethena.text: Ethena's USDe is still the tokenized basis trade, but the current reserve mix is more conservative and more complicated than the original pitch: roughly three quarters liquid stablecoins, about 16% BTC delta-neutral exposure, and about 8% ETH or LST delta-neutral exposure. The liquid-stable sleeve leans heavily on USDtb and therefore BlackRock BUIDL, while the hedged crypto sleeve still depends on off-exchange custody and CEX perpetual markets through venues such as Binance, Bybit, and OKX. Pharos captures the contradiction cleanly: an A+ peg record sitting beside F resilience and D decentralization, which is what happens when the price behaves beautifully but the machinery remains a stack of counterparties. Real-time transparency from Ethena's dashboard helps, but it does not turn CEX custody, backend-signed mint flows, or USDtb-to-BUIDL dependency into neutral facts. The institutional surface area keeps growing regardless — Robinhood's new chain launched with USDe as a primary collateral asset in its Earn program, curated by Steakhouse Financial. USDe's trick is making a risky institutional trade look calm at the token level; the dashboard's job is to keep pointing at the machinery underneath.

aeur-anchored-coins.title: Death of a Swiss Euro
aeur-anchored-coins.text: AEUR is Anchored Coins' centralized euro stablecoin, backed by euro reserves at Swissquote Bank SA, but the issuer is in a regulated wind-down with no new issuance. The FlowBank bankruptcy exposure that once complicated the backing has been resolved through that consolidation, yet the operating posture is permanent: Binance EEA delisted the token and MiCAR-era requirements leave no obvious reactivation path. Thin DEX trading and a large minimum for direct issuer {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} make the peg less something a market can repair than a balance sheet the issuer can settle. The reserves may be intact, but a stablecoin without an active mint-and-distribution loop is a product in hospice care. The rails remain; the reason to use them does not.

buck-bucket-protocol.title: Sui's CDP Experiment
buck-bucket-protocol.text: BUCK is Bucket Protocol's {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} Sui-native dollar stablecoin minted from SUI, BTC, ETH, and LSTs through {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} vaults with {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}} stablecoin swaps. Bucket Protocol brings the MakerDAO playbook to Sui: deposit SUI (45%), USDC/USDT via PSM (25%), wrapped BTC (15%), or ETH/LSTs (15%), mint BUCK at zero interest, get liquidated at 110% collateral ratio. The 90-rated backstop with direct BUCK {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} for collateral provides a strong structural floor, but the 553 depeg events including one that cratered 7,505 basis points below peg reveal what happens when the primary collateral is a volatile L1 token. The F in decentralization at 15 reflects the established-alt-L1 chain penalty, and the PSM module accepting USDC and USDT is a polite way of saying the decentralized stablecoin ultimately leans on centralized ones when it matters. A DEWS score of 2 — among the lowest on the dashboard — suggests the current period is unusually calm for a product whose history includes some of the most severe depegs of any surviving CDP.

vchf-vnx.title: Liechtenstein's Franc Experiment
vchf-vnx.text: VNX's VCHF is a CHF-redeemable stablecoin operating under Liechtenstein's TVTG Blockchain Act with FMA oversight. Its reserve reports establish aggregate CHF-value coverage held in bank and/or securities custody accounts, but do not disclose the holdings or category split: regulated is not the same thing as fully legible. Direct issuer {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} and broad deployment infrastructure give the token more operational scaffolding than its thin on-chain trading demand appears to require. That makes VCHF a competent niche instrument, but not a self-sustaining CHF DeFi market. The question is whether a regulated franc rail finds a use case before its distribution footprint becomes an expensive museum exhibit.

veur-vnx.title: Eleven Chains, Three Users
veur-vnx.text: VEUR stretches across a dozen chains under Liechtenstein FMA Blockchain Act licensing with AREVA-audited euro reserves — wide distribution, tiny gravity. The footprint spans Ethereum, Avalanche, Arbitrum, Base, Polygon, Celo, Solana, XRPL, Tezos, Fraxtal, ICP, and Stellar, which would matter more if the float were not a rounding error beside EURC. The latest live profile has slipped into merely middling territory despite genuine substance: fiat {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, formal {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}, and same-day issuer {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} for KYC customers. Thinly traded non-USD tokens can look worse than their reserve quality, and VEUR is very much living that lesson. MiCA-era competition from SocGen, Banking Circle, and Quantoz makes the FMA license increasingly second-tier in the euro hierarchy. VNX has built the multi-chain plumbing; the market has mostly declined to move in.

audd-novatti.title: Australia's Compliance Play
audd-novatti.text: AUDD is AUDC Pty Ltd's centralized Australian dollar stablecoin, redeemable 1:1 and backed by AUD cash and {{term:treasury}}Treasury bills{{/term}} at regulated Australian banks. AUDD is what happens when a publicly listed fintech (Novatti, on the ASX) builds a stablecoin the way regulators wish everyone would: 100% AUD cash and Treasury bills at Authorised Deposit-taking Institutions, AFSL No. 700123 from ASIC, monthly independent {{term:attestation}}attestations{{/term}} by William Buck, and selection for the Reserve Bank of Australia's Project Acacia pilot. The C+ safety grade reflects solid fundamentals — a B+ peg, B+ resilience, and a stress profile that rarely leaves the calm end of the scale — dragged down by genuinely thin DEX liquidity, where a shallow pool footprint would struggle to absorb any meaningful sell pressure. The dozens of recorded depeg events, with a worst downside near 3,000 basis points, speak to the realities of pricing an AUD-pegged asset against dollar-dominated crypto markets, where FX volatility does the damage that reserve quality cannot prevent. AUDD's challenge was never product quality; it is whether Australia's on-chain economy grows large enough to sustain a domestic stablecoin alternative.

cgusd-cygnus-finance.title: Base's Treasury Wrapper
cgusd-cygnus-finance.text: cgUSD is Cygnus Finance's daily-rebasing T-bill dollar on Base; NAV-vs-price arbitrage friction has produced a long tail of depeg events. The reserve model is clean on paper: 80% off-chain {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}}, 15% on-chain USDC/USDT, and accrued interest, with a Transmuter giving holders instant 1:1 conversion to USDC when it has capacity. The depeg history tells a different story than the treasury-wrapper pitch, because the gap between off-chain NAV and on-chain price creates arbitrage friction the rebase mechanism cannot fully erase. Institutional-unregulated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} with no robust published proof path leaves the trust assumptions sitting mostly with the Cygnus team. Base-only deployment is pragmatic for a USDC-heavy product, but the multi-day settlement window outside the Transmuter means cgUSD's convenience premium is narrower than the wrapper makes it look. The reserve is an {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} basket; the exit experience is still very much a DeFi product.

fxusd-f-x-protocol.title: Leverage as a Peg Mechanism
fxusd-f-x-protocol.text: fxUSD is f(x) Protocol's {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-minted dollar {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} by WBTC and wstETH, with a Stability Pool arbitraging Curve to defend the peg. f(x) Protocol turns leveraged long positions into peg defense: xPOSITION NFTs represent looped exposure to WBTC (58%) and wstETH (42%), while fxUSD holders get the stable side of the trade. The safety grade has slipped to B — still respectable for an $18M crypto-backed stablecoin, but no longer the standout it once was, with WBTC's BitGo/Coinbase custody dragging on an otherwise clever design. It earns its keep through an 89-rated atomic {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop with a 50 bps fee and a Stability Pool that actively arbitrages the USDC/fxUSD Curve pool. Dozens of brief depeg blips, the worst a 291 bps positive deviation, show the mechanism wobbles but recovers. The 3.61% yield from the Stability Pool carries a 0.20 yield-to-risk ratio, the best compensation-per-unit-of-risk among comparable tracked crypto-backed coins. Primary-coverage DEX liquidity is concentrated at 0.52 HHI, meaning one pool failure would gut exit capacity. A clever design that works until vol overwhelms the leverage.

usdb-blast.title: Post-Airdrop Decay
usdb-blast.text: USDB's reserve is quality stablecoin collateral routed through MakerDAO DSR, but the product is stranded on a chain the market stopped caring about post-airdrop. The current metadata models the backing through Blast's DAI yield manager, which is less exotic than the surrounding ecosystem branding would suggest. The long depeg history tells the story of a rebasing stablecoin on an island where liquidity and attention both thinned after incentives faded. Governance-set yield barely registers against the cost of holding a chain-native wrapper with no issuer-style {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop. The safety profile is dragged down by Blast-only deployment and fallback-class secondary liquidity, even though the underlying collateral would look respectable in a more liquid wrapper. USDB is a technically competent product stuck in a room where the party ended and the lights are still on.

buidl-blackrock.title: The Stablecoin's Stablecoin
buidl-blackrock.text: BUIDL is BlackRock's tokenized institutional {{term:money-market-fund}}money-market fund{{/term}}, NAV-pegged to $1 and backed by U.S. {{term:treasury}}Treasuries{{/term}}, repos, and cash custodied by BNY Mellon. It has become the largest tokenized money market fund and the asset that a growing list of stablecoins (USDe, USDtb, frxUSD, USD0, CASH) hold in their own reserves rather than managing T-bill {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} directly. Its B-minus report card is a reminder that Pharos measures structural risk, not brand prestige: institutional-top custody at BNY Mellon and all-very-low-risk reserves earn A+ resilience, but zero DEX liquidity, no recorded depeg events, and Reg D access restrictions confine BUIDL to a world invisible to retail. The roughly 3.5% NAV-appreciation yield net of 20 bps fees is T-bill rate pass-through, unremarkable on its own but compelling when you consider it comes with BlackRock counterparty risk rather than crypto-native smart contract risk. Eight chain deployments via Securitize are expanding the footprint, but BUIDL's true significance is infrastructural — it is the plumbing layer where TradFi yield enters crypto's reserve stacks, not an asset most humans will ever hold directly.

btcusd-btcfi.title: Bitcoin's CDP Outpost
btcusd-btcfi.text: BtcUSD is BTCfi's {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} USD stablecoin minted from BTC variants through Liquity-style {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} vaults. The backing is all Bitcoin exposure in various wrapped or native forms — WBTC, BTCB, cbBTC, and BTC — which gives holders hard-money aesthetics plus every {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} assumption those wrappers drag along. Its long depeg history makes it one of the noisier CDPs per unit of market relevance, even if the live stress signal is not currently screaming. Deployed on Base and Bifrost with no modeled {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop, the practical exit route is secondary-market liquidity on chains the broader DeFi market does not heavily visit. The question remains whether BTC holders will trust yet another wrapping layer when established CDPs already accept wrapped Bitcoin with better liquidity and peg infrastructure.

usbd-bima.title: BTC Collateral, CDP Ambitions
usbd-bima.text: USBD is a Liquity-style BTC-LST {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} stablecoin whose 150% mechanics are undermined by high-risk wrapper collateral and a barely tested secondary market. Bima puts Bitcoin liquid staking and restaking derivatives into overcollateralized vaults, with permissionless {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} for BTC-denominated collateral and a {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}} for near-1:1 stablecoin swaps. The live grade has slipped from the earlier flattering read because the peg can look calm when almost nobody is trading it. The collateral is not plain BTC but a chain of wrappers and restaking derivatives where each layer adds {{term:bridge}}bridge{{/term}} and {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} assumptions the Liquity mechanics were designed to avoid. The permissionless backstop is structurally strong on paper; with no meaningful secondary market, the practical exit remains an open question rather than a settled one.

doc-money-on-chain.title: Bitcoin, Not Bank Deposits
doc-money-on-chain.text: DOC is Money On Chain's rBTC-collateralized USD stablecoin on Rootstock; small, but proof Bitcoin-collateralized dollars are alive outside Ethereum. Dollar on Chain is one of the cleaner hard-money stablecoin designs in the tracked set: no bank reserve story, no fiat {{term:custody}}custodian{{/term}}, just rBTC locked inside Money On Chain and a protocol that lets holders move back into Bitcoin-sidechain collateral when they want out. That simplicity cuts both ways. DOC's reserve logic is easier to trust than most small fiat tokens, but its market depth, chain reach, and surrounding infrastructure are far thinner than mainstream dollar stablecoins. At roughly $5 million in circulation, DOC matters less as a payments network than as proof that Bitcoin-collateralized dollars are still alive outside Ethereum's orbit. Mechanically DOC is a {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} against rBTC with {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} and permissionless {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} for rBTC.

usdrif-rif.title: The RIF-Collateralized Dollar
usdrif-rif.text: USDRIF is a Rootstock {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} stablecoin minted against RIF token collateral — onchain and transparent, but reserve quality is weak relative to BTC-backed alternatives. RIF US Dollar pushes the Rootstock stablecoin experiment further out on the risk curve than DOC: the peg is maintained with RIF collateral rather than Bitcoin collateral, which keeps everything onchain and transparent while making the reserve much weaker in quality. The protocol docs support minting and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} through {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} positions exposed to {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} risk, but the structure is still niche — small, volatile-collateral-backed, and dependent on a market that has never reached real scale. That makes USDRIF worth tracking as a live Rootstock stablecoin, not as a high-confidence safe haven.

isc-international-stable-currency.title: The Anti-Dollar Experiment
isc-international-stable-currency.text: ISC deliberately rejects the dollar peg and tries to stabilize purchasing power through a basket split across gold, investment-grade bonds, short-term T-bills, equities, and cash. That makes it one of the more intellectually honest uses of the word stable: nominal price can drift upward because the target is a basket, not one dollar frozen in amber. The catch is equally direct: Solana-only issuance, institutional-unregulated custody, and a retained freeze authority make the control surface much less elegant than the monetary philosophy. Pharos treats it as a NAV-style RWA token, useful as an inflation argument and awkward as everyday settlement. Being philosophically right is not the same thing as being liquid, which is the part every flatcoin eventually has to learn.

usd0-usual.title: Six Wrappers Deep
usd0-usual.text: USD0 is an RWA-backed dollar layered across USYC, M, USTBL, and USDC, leaning on a strong permissionless redemption backstop. The reserve stack is mostly tokenized {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} and repo exposure, but it reaches holders through other issuers' wrappers, so every supposedly boring component arrives with its own operating model and counterparty chain. That compounding is exactly why the live profile remains middling despite excellent peg behavior: liquidity, dependency, and decentralization do the damage. The market still remembers the USD0++ episode, which proved that clever tokenomics can complicate even a diversified reserve base. The permissionless {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} path through DaoCollateral is the structural saving grace, but recurring small depeg blips show secondary-market confidence can still wobble. France-domiciled, RWA-backed, and architecturally ambitious, USD0 remains a bet that several low-risk parts do not add up to one meaningfully riskier whole.

usr-resolv.title: Insurance Layer, Meet Reality
usr-resolv.text: Resolv's USR was a {{term:delta-neutral}}delta-neutral{{/term}} synthetic dollar with an RLP insurance layer; it collapsed in 2026 after an EOA-minter exploit produced 80M unbacked tokens and depegged the asset, and the token was frozen. Resolv's USR was a {{term:basis-trade}}basis trade{{/term}}-driven synthetic dollar whose RLP insurance layer was supposed to absorb negative {{term:funding-rate}}funding rate{{/term}} pressure and protect USR holders — until an EOA-minter exploit produced 80M unbacked tokens and shattered the peg. By the time of the freeze, USR had collapsed to $0.164 — an 83.6% deviation from its dollar target — and 25 depeg events including a worst of 9,025 basis points sat on the permanent record. Supply was volatile in the months leading up to the failure, swinging from $17.5M to $28.4M to $22.3M, the kind of oscillation that suggested frantic positioning rather than organic growth. The irony was sharp: Apostro real-time reserve verification and permissionless atomic {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} with an 82-rated backstop were still technically intact on a token trading at sixteen cents before being frozen. {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} of the {{term:delta-neutral}}delta-neutral{{/term}} margin via off-exchange settlement partners did not save the synthetic when the EOA minter was compromised. Six-chain deployment across Ethereum, Base, BSC, Berachain, HyperEVM, and Arbitrum meant the failure was visible everywhere, not just somewhere.

usdz-anzen.title: Private Credit Meets DeFi
usdz-anzen.text: Anzen's USDz is 80% backed by U.S. private credit ABS — SMB merchant receivables, factored invoices, auto leases, consumer installment lending, and litigation finance — underwritten by SEC-licensed broker-dealer Percent, with 15% in Superstate tokenized {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} products and 5% cash. A mediocre peg grade and hundreds of recorded depeg events make USDz one of the more frequently depegged stablecoins on the dashboard, and its supply has contracted sharply, answering the question of what happens when holders lose confidence in private credit backing. Qualified Market Makers mint at 1:1 USDz/USDC while retail relies on DEX arbitrage to close the gap — a two-tier system that works when the market trusts the collateral and breaks when it doesn't. The yield from private credit is real and uncorrelated with crypto markets, but so is the liquidity mismatch between 90-day {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} receivables and instant {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} expectations against {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}-only proof.

ausd-agora.title: VanEck's Quiet Dollar
ausd-agora.text: AUSD is Agora's centralized dollar stablecoin, redeemable 1:1 and backed by cash, short-dated U.S. {{term:treasury}}Treasury bills{{/term}}, and overnight repos managed by VanEck. The institutional stack is unusually explicit: VanEck manages the reserves, State Street provides {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} through a bankruptcy-remote Delaware Statutory Trust, and Grant Thornton publishes monthly {{term:attestation}}reserve attestations{{/term}} rather than a token-specific real-time proof feed. Revenue sharing with distribution partners has helped its multichain rollout without changing the basic bargain: holders rely on an issuer, an asset manager, a custodian, and a periodic accountant. That is a cleaner chain than many fiat-backed dollars offer, but it is still a chain. AUSD's transparency is monthly-attestation based, not a live on-chain reserve window.

usds-sky.title: The PSM Moat Deepens
usds-sky.text: Sky Dollar still commands the single best {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} infrastructure in stablecoins: a permissionless {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}} with atomic, zero-fee settlement and well over half of total supply available as immediate exit capacity — no other stablecoin at scale offers anything close. The A- safety grade reflects strength tempered by where the cracks actually are, with a reserve mix split across PSM stablecoins, Spark lending {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} positions, and Grove {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} allocations providing genuine diversification rather than the concentration risk that plagues most competitors. The peg itself is the easy part — USDS sits at the calm end of the stress scale and clears its worst sub-day wobbles within hours, with only a handful of brief deviations across the rolling window. The yield-to-risk story through the Sky Savings Rate still rewards holders without the exotic risk profiles that higher-yielding alternatives require. The structural dependency on USDC as mechanism-critical PSM collateral remains the one tension in a DAO-governed system that aspires to monetary sovereignty — roughly a third of Sky Dollar's backing ultimately traces back to Circle's banking relationships, with {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} Maker vaults backing the rest.

m-m0.title: The Middleware Dollar
m-m0.text: Institutional dollar stablecoin minted 1:1 by permissioned issuers against short-term U.S. T-bills in bankruptcy-remote SPVs, with on-chain validator attestations replacing periodic audits; institution-facing liquidity offset by issuer redeemability. M0's M token is backed 100% by short-term {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}} in bankruptcy-remote SPVs — a pristine reserve that earns a perfect peg score, yet the overall safety grade sits at C: the redeemability backstop and clean collateral are dragged down by centralized governance and institutional-unregulated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}. The tension is the familiar one: direct M liquidity stays institution-facing rather than pooled on DEXes, so Pharos leaves it unrated on liquidity, but eventual {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} gives the token a stronger exit profile than spot depth alone would suggest. Permissioned Minters lock T-bill collateral while Validators cryptographically attest sufficiency on-chain, a trust architecture that swaps auditor snapshots for protocol-level verification — elegant, but it concentrates control in a permissioned issuer set, which is exactly what holds the grade down. M's significance is downstream: it anchors the M0 infrastructure cohort that powers Noble's USDN, MetaMask's mUSD, USD.AI's USDai, Usual's USD0, and wrapped M integrations.

usdm-moneta.title: Peg in Name Only
usdm-moneta.text: Moneta's USDM is the dashboard's cleanest example of pristine reserves failing to create a usable peg. The backing is regulator-friendly: 60% {{term:money-market-fund}}money-market funds{{/term}} from Fidelity and Amundi, 40% USD bank deposits, Norwegian MiCA EMT licensing, and a Charli3 oracle {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} before each Cardano mint. The problem is brutally simple: with no meaningful observable DEX liquidity, there are no arbitrageurs to enforce the peg, so the price wanders wherever thin order books take it. The live score is still failing even if the exact number moves around, because reserve quality is not the broken part. Multi-day issuer settlement compounds the exit risk for anyone holding meaningful size. USDM is a well-backed IOU trading at whatever the market feels like, which is a stablecoin only in the most technical and least comforting sense.

satusd-river.title: The Purist's CDP
satusd-river.text: River's satUSD is a purist Omni-CDP that refuses centralized stablecoin collateral and accepts BTC, ETH, BNB, and LSTs only. That stance gives it a clean dependency story, but peg stability has paid the price through a long record of secondary-market wobble. The Omni-{{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} architecture lets users deposit collateral on one chain and mint satUSD on another through LayerZero {{term:bridge}}bridging{{/term}}, which expands distribution while importing the usual cross-chain assumptions. The {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop offers permissionless access to blue-chip collateral through {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} positions, but minimal DEX liquidity across many chains leaves the secondary market paper-thin. Decentralized governance helps the ideology column; unproven-chain sprawl and fragile liquidity keep the score from turning that ideology into comfort. satUSD is the most principled CDP in its lane, and the market keeps reminding it that principles are not bids.

usdf-astherus.title: One Exchange, One Exit
usdf-astherus.text: Astherus USDF is a Binance-routed {{term:basis-trade}}basis-trade{{/term}} stablecoin via Ceffu MirrorX — single-CEX concentration risk where the {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop, collateral, and hedge all run through one pipeline. USDF routes its entire existence through Binance: 50% USDT held in Ceffu {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, 25% spot crypto longs, and 25% perpetual short positions — all executed via Ceffu's MirrorX infrastructure on a single centralized exchange. The peg itself is the easy part, and the dashboard agrees: it holds an A+ peg grade and the day-to-day stress signal sits glued to the calm end of the scale, having logged only a handful of brief, modest deviations over the tracking window. The danger here is structural, not market-visible, and the C- overall safety grade reflects it — resilience grades an outright F, because BSC-only deployment with thin single-pool DEX liquidity means on-chain exit options are essentially decorative the moment the Binance-Ceffu pipeline that holds the collateral, runs the hedge, and gates redemptions ever hiccups. USDF is a {{term:delta-neutral}}delta-neutral{{/term}} yield product wearing a stablecoin's clothes, and the single point of failure is the entire wardrobe.

usda-avalon.title: The BTC-Backed Misnomer
usda-avalon.text: Avalon USDa calls itself a BTC-backed CDP, but the reserve mix is messier: FBTC custody exposure, a large USDT leg, and assorted BTC LSTs all sit under the Bitcoin banner. The design adds 1:1 USDT convertibility, Redstone-priced collateral, HFT liquidation machinery, and LayerZero bridge distribution, which is a lot of plumbing for a token marketed as simple Bitcoin-backed dollars. Pharos keeps the collateral-quality view conservative because wrapped BTC, centralized stablecoin exposure, and permissioned mint controls are not the same thing as holding native BTC in a trustless vault. The interesting contradiction is that the liquidation machinery can look sophisticated while the holder still depends on Cobo, Fireblocks, Coinbase Prime, role-gated minting, and cross-chain infrastructure behaving well at the same time. Lately the room has been emptying: supply has roughly halved inside a month — the Ethereum leg alone shrank by nine figures — while the token trades persistently soft of the dollar and price coverage has thinned enough that the report card now reads F across peg and liquidity. Nobody published a post-mortem; the exits are simply visible on-chain. It is a Bitcoin stablecoin in the way a finance committee is a wallet: technically connected to the asset, heavily mediated by everyone in the room.

usdtb-ethena.title: The Load-Bearing Wall
usdtb-ethena.text: USDtb is the stable ballast in Ethena's reserve structure, designed chiefly to be held by its parent protocol rather than traded as a retail DeFi dollar. Its reserve is mostly BlackRock's BUIDL, with cash or cash-equivalent redemption reserves, issued by Anchorage Digital and held with U.S. Bank. That puts short-dated U.S. {{term:treasury}}Treasuries{{/term}} behind the token, but through a deliberately long chain of funds, custodians, issuer controls, and Ethena risk management. Direct mint-and-redeem rails and BUIDL's atomic redemption are useful exits, though they do not turn the product into a broadly liquid consumer asset. USDtb is sensible collateral for a system that wants a quiet corner of traditional finance, and a reminder that every quiet corner has several doors.

zeusd-zoth.title: Wrappers All the Way Down
zeusd-zoth.text:
A CDP minted against tokenized T-bills layered on tokenized T-bills — an F-grade reserve dependency chain with $1.5K of DEX liquidity backing $27.6M of supply.

ZeUSD mints as a {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} against a collateral stack of tokenized T-bills (USYC, STBT, TBILL), Usual's USD0++, and wrapped M — every dollar of {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} backing carries the risk profile of whichever upstream issuer is weakest in the chain. The F at 35 is the predictable result: Cayman domicile, no proof of reserves, institutional-unregulated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, and a dependency chain where a failure in Hashnote, Matrixdock, or OpenEden cascades directly into ZeUSD's reserve. The $1,486 in DEX TVL across a single pool is not a liquidity problem — it is the absence of liquidity entirely, leaving $27.6M in circulating supply with no meaningful on-chain exit. Zero depeg events and a calm DEWS band mean the peg hasn't been tested, not that it would survive testing. The RWA-collateralized CDP model is architecturally interesting, but wrapping three layers of tokenized treasuries into a fourth token is the kind of financial engineering that works until it doesn't.

zchf-frankencoin.title: Oracle-Free Alpine Defiance
zchf-frankencoin.text:
A CHF-pegged CDP with auction-priced collateral, no oracle dependency, no team tokens, and a safety grade that has slipped to B- as the collateral mix has drifted away from its crypto-and-gold roots.

Frankencoin remains the most ideologically committed stablecoin on the dashboard — no foundation, no team tokens, no VC money, no price oracles — and that orthodoxy still earns it a top-tier decentralization mark. But the overall B- grade is another step down from where it once sat, and the reason is sitting in the collateral pool: a single corporate equity, BOSS (Boss Info AG), now makes up roughly a third of the backing — rivaling wrapped BTC as the largest position and introducing issuer- and liquidity-specific risk the crypto and gold lines never carried. The collateral is still valued through auction-based {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} that trades capital efficiency for oracle manipulation resistance, a tradeoff most {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} protocols wouldn't dare make, and {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} is enforced through veto-governed minting limits — but governance has plainly let the mix tilt toward a riskier single name. The peg itself is unbothered, holding near-perfect with only a handful of shallow deviations under 230 bps and rarely straying from the calm end of the stress scale, which is genuinely impressive for a CHF token priced against dollar reference rates on thin liquidity. A MiCA whitepaper filed in the EU register days before the July 1 transition deadline keeps ZCHF on regulated European shelves — pragmatism from the purists, timed to the wire. The 3.5% APY from Frankencoin Savings remains a rare risk-adjusted draw for a non-USD stablecoin, but the widening gap between Frankencoin's decentralization purity and its collateral discipline is the thing to watch from here.

usn-noon.title: Yield Portfolio, Base Token
usn-noon.text: Noon's USN is the base dollar in a yield machine that would prefer you notice the par wrapper before the credit stack. Pharos metadata shows reserves spread across private credit, CLO exposure, DeFi lending, principal tokens, and a small Treasury-bill sleeve, with Accountable providing a real-time reserve feed. Base USN does not itself accrue the yield; that job belongs to sUSN, while USN holders still rely on the same permissioned mint and redemption machinery. The setup is more transparent than many credit-backed dollars, but transparency is not a guarantee that private-credit liquidity arrives politely during stress. USN is stablecoin-shaped, yet the balance sheet underneath reads more like an institutional yield portfolio with a dollar label taped to the front.

honey-berachain.title: Proof of Liquidity's Dollar
honey-berachain.text: 1:1 basket-backed dollar on Berachain (USDC/USDT0/pyUSD/USDe) with atomic basket unwind; chain immaturity and dependency drag the grade into D territory. HONEY is Berachain's native stablecoin, minted 1:1 against a basket of USDC, USDT0, pyUSD, and USDe through permissionless on-chain vaults governed by BGT holders. The redemption backstop with atomic settlement is the headline: you can always unwind HONEY into its constituent stablecoins, which is more than most basket tokens offer, and the peg itself has held tight enough to stay at the calm end of the stress scale. But the D safety grade is no accident — a fully centralized-dependent governance posture, reliance on those upstream issuers, and Berachain's unproven status all compound, and the dozens of brief sub-50-bps blips plus one absurd +4,981 bps upward spike show the chaos beneath the surface in the ecosystem's early days. That kind of upward deviation points to thin two-sided liquidity rather than a backing failure, and the modest effective depth relative to headline TVL confirms much of the on-chain liquidity is shallow. The underlying basket architecture would score meaningfully higher on an established chain with less concentrated control; here it reads as a sound mechanism wearing its host's risks. Structurally, HONEY's basket mint and Basket Mode work like a multi-asset {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}}, with permissionless atomic {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} into its underlying stablecoin reserves.

wusd-worldwide.title: Enterprise Rails, Empty Station
wusd-worldwide.text:
WSPN's white-label dollar pairs conservative T-bill reserves with a C+ grade and thin DEX liquidity that betrays missing on-chain demand.

WSPN's Worldwide USD pairs a conservative reserve — {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}} and cash with a Basel III-inspired 6% liquidity buffer — against a C+ safety grade that reflects the gap between institutional ambition and on-chain traction. The peg itself holds clean and rarely strays from the calm end of the stress scale, but liquidity is the soft spot: the DEX float across Ethereum, Polygon, and Viction is too thin to absorb size, and a couple of shallow sub-200-bps wobbles suggest the peg holds because almost nothing tests it. The BVI domicile with FinCEN MSB registration is regulatory limbo: enough paperwork to look legitimate, not enough to satisfy institutional compliance departments shopping for USDC alternatives. WUSD's white-label infrastructure for enterprise stablecoin issuance is the real product pitch, but a payments network needs volume, and volume needs liquidity that isn't here yet — and the {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} story alone won't fix that.

frxusd-frax.title: Frax's Clean Slate
frxusd-frax.text: frxUSD is Frax's tokenized-{{term:treasury}}T-bill{{/term}}-backed dollar minted and redeemed 1:1 through governance-approved custodians, a {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} do-over without legacy FRAX's algorithmic baggage. Its reserves span tokenized government-money products and fiat-backed dollars including BUIDL, USTB, USCC, JTRSY, WTGXX, AUSD, and USDC, while the enshrined-custodian design gives users a direct exit whenever the relevant collateral is available. The sfrxUSD wrapper passes through reserve yield, which is modestly useful and mercifully not the whole pitch. The trade-off is concentration in a small club of tokenized-money issuers, plus Frax DAO's power to approve the custodians. It is institutional plumbing arranged by a crypto protocol: much tidier than old FRAX, but not magically free of gatekeepers.

usyc-hashnote.title: Circle USYC Goes Multichain
usyc-hashnote.text: USYC is Hashnote's tokenized short-duration fund share now wearing Circle's distribution jacket. The reserve mix is the clean TradFi part: mostly U.S. Treasury bills with reverse repo agreements, redeemable at NAV rather than pretending every token is a static dollar bill. That NAV behavior matters because USYC is yield-bearing fund exposure, not a payment stablecoin, and Pharos treats the issuer controls accordingly. Circle's rebrand and multichain push make the wrapper easier to move around, but the legal and operational substance remains fund administration, eligible access, and issuer-operated minting. It is a very respectable money-market instrument cosplaying just enough as crypto to become collateral elsewhere.

eurr-stablr.title: Malta's Euro Bet
eurr-stablr.text: EURR is StablR's Malta MFSA MiCA euro stablecoin with Grant Thornton {{term:attestation}}attestations{{/term}} — distinguished mostly by Tether's strategic backing. StablR's EURR is backed 100% by fiat euro at European financial institutions under a Malta MFSA EMI license with MiCA compliance and Grant Thornton attestations — the same regulatory infrastructure as its dollar sibling USDR, with Tether's strategic investment providing both capital and the awkward question of whether a Tether-backed entity can win institutional trust in a market built on regulatory purity. Compliance stopped being a differentiator in May 2026, when an attacker compromised StablR's 1-of-3 minting multisig and printed 4.5 million unbacked EURR alongside millions in USDR — the token broke as low as the mid-$0.50s, minting and redemption were frozen, and StablR had to tell Malta's MFSA that supply was no longer fully backed. The strange coda: after the EU's MiCA transition closed on July 1, EURR still stood among the handful of authorized euro stablecoins — hacked, suspended, and compliant all at once, while the report card reads F.
