The project recently completed an external audit that surfaced a high-severity LP token price manipulation vulnerability and a medium-severity timelock bypass, both now remediated with fuzz testing added — the kind of findings that are routine for a Liquity fork adapting to exotic collateral types but worth watching post-launch. Still in the auditing phase with a Q2 2026 target, Base Dollar is betting that LP-collateralized debt positions can offer better capital efficiency than vanilla ETH CDPs, though the trade-off is inheriting every smart contract risk in the Aerodrome stack on top of its own.

wm-m0.title: The Plumbing's Plumbing
wm-m0.text: wM is M0's non-rebasing ERC-20 wrapper over M, backed by short-term U.S. {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} bills in bankruptcy-remote SPVs — holders forfeit the yield, which routes to TTG-approved earner accounts. wM is the non-rebasing wrapper that turns M0's {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}}-bill token into something a normal ERC-20 contract can hold without breaking — and the price of that convenience is that holders volunteer to forfeit the yield. Underneath sits the same 30-to-90-day {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} bills, the same bankruptcy-remote SPVs, the same Validator {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} as M itself, but the WrappedMToken contract routes all accrued yield to TTG-approved earner accounts (read: the downstream M0 ecosystem — USDat, USDSC, ctUSD, mUSD, USD0, and friends) via claimExcess(), leaving wM holders with a flat dollar that does nothing. There is no blacklist, no freeze, no pause function — a refreshingly minimal surface for a centralized stablecoin built on {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} collateral — and wrap/unwrap are open and free, so the peg holds by pure arbitrage against M. At roughly $93M in circulation across Ethereum, Arbitrum, Plume, and Solana, wM is the composability primitive the entire M0 ecosystem builds on top of: nobody is meant to hold it directly, everyone is meant to hold something built from it. It is the cleanest expression of M0's thesis that yield belongs to whoever bothers to put the dollar to work, not to whoever happens to be holding it when the music stops.

usdnr-nerona.title: A Private Bank for Five Wallets
usdnr-nerona.text: Nerona's USDnr is a $50M M0-wrapper stablecoin held by exactly five wallets, with permissioned KYC-gated {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} — the T-bill carry accrues to Nerona, not holders. Nerona USD is a $50M M0-wrapper stablecoin issued by a private-wealth-management startup that has so far convinced exactly five wallets to hold it — a holder count more befitting a family office than a stablecoin. The token is structurally a thin wrapper over M0's $M (collateralised by Superstate's USTB {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} fund and minted by MXON), and despite Nerona's marketing copy promising capital that 'works while you don't', USDnr itself is non-yield-bearing: the T-bill carry accrues to the M0 reserve and Nerona, not to holders. Governance is single-entity, redemption is permissioned and KYC-gated, and the wrapper inherits every M0-layer risk — minter insolvency, M0 governance deactivation, and the small matter of being unregulated. Mind the symbol: this is USDnr (Nerona, on Ethereum), not USDN (Noble's M0-wrapper on Cosmos) — sloppy press copy and screenshots conflate the two, but they share nothing beyond the M0 plumbing underneath. A private bank for the onchain era, with a circulating-supply-to-holders ratio that rounds to $10M per client.

usdk-kast.title: The Anjouan Card Dollar
usdk-kast.text: KAST's USDK is an Anjouan-domiciled M0 wrapper of tokenized {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}}, distributed via a fintech card app — T-bill yield is retained by KAST, not passed to holders. KAST Dollar is what you get when a Comoros-domiciled fintech wraps M0's tokenized {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}}, slaps a card on top, and quietly pockets the yield. The token sits on Solana as a Token-2022 mint with permissioned transfer hooks and confidential-transfer extensions built in — useful if you trust KAST and BitGo, awkward otherwise. At roughly $24M outstanding it is still proof-of-concept scale, riding entirely on M0 Validator {{term:attestation}}attestations{{/term}} rather than its own audit trail. Holders earn nothing; if you want the T-bill carry you're nudged into USDKy, KAST's separately rebasing twin. The legal stack — KAST Tech in Anjouan, {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} by partners, 'not a bank' disclaimer in bold — is the modern offshore neobank uniform. A cleaner version of buying T-bills than most card-app stablecoins, provided you've made peace with single-jurisdiction issuer risk and a regulator most maps don't bother to label.

xo-exodus.title: Self-Custody's Custodial Dollar
xo-exodus.text:
MoonPay mints, M0 wraps, Exodus distributes — a Treasury-backed Solana token whose yield accrues to issuers and whose authorities live on a single MoonPay key.

When a self-custody wallet best known for letting users hold their own keys decides to mint its own dollar, the result is XO Cash: a MoonPay-issued, M0-wrapped {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} claim wearing an Exodus hoodie. The reserves sit in MoonPay's regulated SPVs under institutional {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} and the M0 yield quietly accrues to the issuers, not the holders, which is the polite way of saying XO is a payment rail with a stablecoin garnish. Token-2022 ships with pausable, transfer-hook, and permanent-delegate authorities all held by a single MoonPay key, so the 'self-custody' marketing applies to your wallet but not to your tokens. Initial proof of product-market fit was paying X Games athletes $2,500 signing bonuses, which is either a charming retail use case or a launch metric in search of a thesis. Backed by short-dated Treasuries, geofenced where it has to be, and aimed squarely at the Exodus Pay card audience that has never asked what an SPV is.

jpysc-sbi-startale.title: Japan's Trust-Bank Yen Goes Live
jpysc-sbi-startale.text: JPYSC went live on June 24, 2026 — Japan's first stablecoin issued through a trust bank rather than under JPYC's prepaid-instrument workaround, and that distinction is still the entire product. Shinsei Trust & Banking issues, SBI VC Trade distributes, and Startale Group (the Astar Network operator and Sony's Soneium co-developer) built the rails, with roughly $63M of cash-and-JGB reserves segregated in trust accounts on day one. The Type III electronic payment instrument classification gives JPYSC what JPYC spent three years negotiating around: trust-law redemption rights, asset segregation, exemption from the ¥1M transfer cap, and permission to park up to 50% of reserves in Japanese government bonds — yield the prepaid model legally can't touch. The catch is that 'launch' means a closed loop. For now only verified SBI VC Trade account holders can hold JPYSC, with no external-wallet withdrawals and no public-chain circulation; Startale insists the on-chain plumbing is built and merely waiting on legal and tax clarity, not technology. So JPYSC is live and untradeable at the same time — a regulated yen token that exists on-chain but can't yet leave the building, which is precisely the bet: that Japan's stablecoin market was gated on legal infrastructure, and SBI's institutional book plus Startale's stack is the right hand to play the moment the gate opens. The trust-bank framework legalizes up to 50% JGB {{term:treasury}}treasury bonds{{/term}} in reserves, trust-segregated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, FSA-grade {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}, and statutory {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} rights.

rgbp-revolut.title: 13 Million Users, One Brand Ban Away
rgbp-revolut.text:
Revolut's pre-launch UK GBP stablecoin is expected to issue from the e-money subsidiary, not the bank, and remains sandbox-only until October 2027 — with proposed BoE rules that legal analysts call structurally unviable.

Revolut got its full UK banking licence on March 11 after a 20-month mobilisation — and then confirmed its proposed GBP stablecoin would not be issued from the new banking entity. Bank of England rules prohibit a UK bank and its affiliated group from issuing stablecoins across different subsidiaries, so issuance falls back to Revolut Ltd, the e-money entity. That structural wrinkle is the smaller of Revolut's UK regulatory headaches. At the House of Lords on March 25, Head of UK Policy Rory Tanner told peers the UK is 'already behind' the US and EU — and flagged the BoE's proposed ban on 'branded' stablecoins as a commercial blocker (the issuer couldn't put its own name on the token). Priority use case per Tanner: the UK→India remittance corridor, the seventh-largest in the world, not retail payments. The FCA sandbox cohort Revolut joined on Feb 25 is testing phase only; the full UK authorisation regime doesn't activate until October 2027, and the BoE's proposed 40% unremunerated-reserve requirement plus £20,000 individual-holder cap describe a commercial model that UK legal analysts call structurally unviable. Revolut's real asset isn't the token — it's 13 million UK users who already open the app daily, with the bank-style {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} stack the issuer plans to bolt on top. Whether that distribution survives the BoE rulebook is the actual question.

ausdt-tether-alloy.title: Gold Collateral, Dollar Target
ausdt-tether-alloy.text: aUSDT is Alloy by Tether's dollar stablecoin — a {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} where verified users deposit Tether Gold (XAUT) and mint dollars at up to 75% LTV, so the peg sits on top of {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} gold rather than a bank account. Alloy Tether turns Tether Gold into a dollar-tracking credit instrument: verified users deposit XAUT into an Ethereum vault, mint aUSDT against a 75% mint-to-value ceiling, and return aUSDT plus fees to withdraw collateral. That gives Pharos a clean on-chain reserve view because the XAUT backing sits in the CMPVault, but it also means aUSDT inherits Tether Gold {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, gold-price volatility, whitelist access, and {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} mechanics. The peg is not a bank-account promise; it is an overcollateralized gold position engineered to trade near one dollar. It is also now a position in run-off: Tether is winding down the Alloy platform, new minting is halted, and holders have until mid-September 2026 to return aUSDT and pull their XAUT collateral before the exit window closes. The experiment ends as a footnote to Tether's gold strategy — the market wanted the bullion token, not a dollar derivative of it.

usdsui-sui.title: Sui Gets Its Native Dollar
usdsui-sui.text: USDsui is Sui's native dollar issued through Bridge (Stripe), backed by short-dated {{term:treasury}}Treasuries{{/term}}/repos/MMFs — a native fiat-backed dollar rather than a bridged USDC. USDsui is the Sui ecosystem dollar issued through Bridge, Stripe's stablecoin infrastructure arm. The asset gives Sui a native fiat-backed stablecoin rather than another {{term:bridge}}bridged{{/term}} dollar, with DefiLlama exposing supply and price data for live peg monitoring. The reserve model is conventional Bridge Open Issuance: cash, short-dated {{term:treasury}}Treasuries{{/term}}, repos, and government {{term:money-market-fund}}money-market funds{{/term}} support mint and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}}, with institutional {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}. DefiLlama supply and price data support peg monitoring, while reserve composition remains curated until Bridge publishes a USDsui-specific reserve feed or Sui supply data with stronger public verification.

brlv-crown.title: Brazilian Bonds On Chain
brlv-crown.text: BRLV is Crown's centralized Brazilian real stablecoin, mint/redeemed 1:1 for BRL and backed mostly by Brazilian federal {{term:treasury}}Treasury bonds{{/term}} in segregated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}. Crown BRLV is a Brazilian real stablecoin backed by federal government bonds pledged for token holders through a security-agent structure. That is a cleaner reserve story than most emerging-market fiat coins: the backing is local sovereign debt rather than offshore dollar liquidity, and the legal structure is designed to keep reserve claims separate from Crown itself. The risks are equally specific: BRL liquidity, Brazilian sovereign-rate volatility, and KYC-gated {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}}. Pharos tracks the BRL peg directly while treating reserves as curated-validated evidence because Crown's reserve page is not yet suitable for automated reserve verification.

usdglo-glo.title: Public-Goods Float
usdglo-glo.text: Glo Dollar is Brale-issued dollar plumbing with an unusual allocation decision: reserve yield funds public-goods causes instead of being rebated to holders, exchanges, or the issuer's distribution partners. The backing itself is deliberately ordinary, split between cash-like assets and U.S. government-backed debt with monthly attestations and 1:1 mint and redemption through Brale. That makes USDGLO's differentiation moral and distributional, not mechanical, which is more interesting than another fake innovation label. Pharos also tracks it because small stablecoins can still become meaningful dependencies when they show up inside other reserve stacks. Commercially inconvenient is currently winning: the float halved inside a month, most of it leaving Celo in a single week, and redirected yield only works when there is a float to redirect. USDGLO is not trying to out-engineer Circle; it is trying to redirect the float, which is both noble and commercially inconvenient.

usdon-ondo.title: Ondo Settlement Cash
usdon-ondo.text: USDon is the cash leg inside Ondo Global Markets, not a retail dollar trying to win every DEX pair on the internet. It is backed by U.S. dollar cash or cash equivalents in brokerage accounts and used to settle purchases and redemptions for tokenized assets under Ondo's regulated platform structure. That gives it cleaner collateral than many RWA-labeled experiments, but also whitelisted access, platform dependency, and issuer-admin controls that keep the risk model institutional. Pharos treats redemption as a Global Markets route rather than a permissionless on-chain backstop, which is the right amount of boring. USDon is settlement cash with a ticker, and pretending otherwise would only make the spreadsheet feel more exciting.

audm-macropod.title: Australia's New On-Chain Dollar
audm-macropod.text: AUDM is Macropod's centralized Australian dollar stablecoin, redeemable 1:1 by approved clients and backed by AUD cash held in segregated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} at Westpac and Banking Circle Australia. Macropod AUDM brings an Australian-dollar unit into the active Pharos set with DefiLlama supply, CoinGecko pricing, Ethereum, Solana, and Redbelly contracts, and issuer documentation describing segregated AUD reserve accounts at Australian ADIs. The product is straightforward: approved Macropod clients can mint and redeem through the platform, with current reserves split mostly between Westpac and Banking Circle Australia, and primary {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} gated to approved clients. The main constraints are scale and disclosure cadence. Pharos can monitor the AUD peg immediately and validate live token supply, while stronger reserve automation depends on recurring machine-readable monthly reports.

audf-forte.title: Australia's New Regulated Long Tail
audf-forte.text: AUDF is Forte Tech Solutions' centralized Australian dollar stablecoin, redeemable 1:1 with AUD reserves and cash-equivalent assets held in segregated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}. Forte AUD is the straightforward version of an Australian stablecoin: issuer-run, AFSL-regulated, publicly documented, and redeemable back into bank-account AUD for eligible users. The reserve story is respectable for a long-tail fiat token because Forte publishes recurring reserve reports and legal terms instead of treating backing as a black box, but the public evidence is still PDF-based rather than a continuously queryable feed. At roughly $3.6 million in market cap, AUDF is not systemically important; the primary path back to fiat is issuer {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} for eligible users. It is interesting because the legal and reserve posture is cleaner than many niche fiat coins even while the liquidity footprint remains small.

busd0-usual.title: Fixed-Maturity USD0 Bond
busd0-usual.text: bUSD0 is Usual's bond-leg wrapper of USD0; before maturity it behaves like a discount bond, not a spot dollar. bUSD0 is Usual's fixed-notional USD0 bond, formerly USD0++, with a June 11, 2028 maturity. It is backed by locked USD0 but does not behave like a spot stablecoin before maturity: par exit requires both bUSD0 and the separate rt-bUSD0 early-exit right, while secondary-market bUSD0 can trade below one dollar. Yield is paid through USUAL coupons rather than dollar NAV growth, so the risk is a mix of USD0 reserve quality, Usual DAO parameter risk, and liquidity/discount risk before maturity. Par {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} requires both tokens, and the underlying USD0 reserve is itself an {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} claim.

susde-ethena.title: Ethena's Savings Sleeve
susde-ethena.text: sUSDe is the yield wrapper over USDe, converting Ethena staking rewards into a rising exchange rate rather than a separate payout. Economically it inherits the same USDe reserve and custody stack: liquid stablecoin backing, delta-neutral BTC and ETH/LST hedges, off-exchange custody, CEX execution, and the operational choreography that keeps the synthetic dollar flat. The wrapper's separate risk is exit timing, because unstaking burns the receipt immediately while the holder still waits through Ethena's cooldown flow before receiving liquid USDe. Pharos therefore treats sUSDe as a wrapper dependency, not a diversified asset that magically escapes the parent risk. It is USDe with yield accounting and a waiting room, which is useful as long as nobody confuses the waiting room for a fire exit.

susds-sky.title: The Plain Sky Savings Token
susds-sky.text: sUSDS is the plain savings receipt in the Sky stack: deposit USDS, receive an ERC-4626-style token whose exchange rate compounds with the Sky Savings Rate. That simplicity is the point, especially next to stUSDS, which pushes holders into risk-capital exposure and borrower shortfall risk. The wrapper still inherits the USDS reserve mix, Sky governance, and the USDS PSM exit surface, so it is not detached from the parent system just because the vault interface is clean. Pharos reads sUSDS as the clean yield-bearing expression of Sky's base dollar, not a separate reserve design. Sometimes the least theatrical wrapper is the one doing the least damage, which in stablecoins is a compliment.

sdai-sky.title: The Classic DSR Wrapper
sdai-sky.text:
The original Dai savings receipt — deposit DAI, accrue the DSR through a rising exchange rate, with wrapper-contract risk on top of DAI-tier CDP risk.

sDAI is the original Dai savings receipt: deposit DAI, receive a token whose redeemable DAI balance grows with the Dai Savings Rate. It adds very little conceptual complexity beyond the base asset, but it still belongs on its own row because holders are choosing a NAV-appreciating {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} wrapper with its own liquidity, integrations, and wrapper-contract risk rather than plain DAI — and the underlying still inherits DAI's {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} collateral profile.

sfrxusd-frax.title: Frax's Yield Sleeve
sfrxusd-frax.text: sfrxUSD is the savings sleeve for frxUSD, not a second Frax dollar with its own reserve book. Depositors trade the flat base token for a vault share whose exchange rate rises as Frax routes frxUSD income and custodian yield into the wrapper. That distinction matters: wrapper risk is share accounting, redemption mechanics, and liquidity for sfrxUSD, while the parent stablecoin risk remains the frxUSD custodian and reserve stack. The multichain footprint makes the token easier to hold, but it also turns a simple Treasury-style reserve story into Frax governance, issuer controls, and bridge-aware exit math wearing a tidy yield label.

scrvusd-curve.title: Borrower Interest Receipt
scrvusd-curve.text: scrvUSD is Curve's ERC-4626 savings share over crvUSD, so the wrapper adds yield and exchange-rate behavior without inventing a new dollar. Deposited crvUSD backs the share, while borrower interest and protocol revenue make the redeemable crvUSD balance climb over time. The wrapper risk is vault accounting, liquidity, and the ability to exit back into crvUSD; the parent risk is still Curve's CDP and LLAMMA machinery, with BTC and ETH collateral doing the heavy lifting underneath. It is the polite version of leverage plumbing: cleaner to hold than raw crvUSD, but absolutely not detached from the machinery that mints the base asset.

cusdo-openeden.title: Non-Rebasing OpenDollar
cusdo-openeden.text: cUSDO is OpenEden's non-rebasing wrapper for USDO, built for protocols that would rather watch a price rise than reconcile changing balances. It keeps the same underlying OpenDollar claim, where USDO is backed by tokenized Treasury exposure and issuer-controlled redemption rails, but moves the yield expression into NAV appreciation. That makes the product mechanically useful without making the reserve chain any shorter: cUSDO still depends on USDO, OpenEden, and the underlying tokenized T-bill stack. The wrapper admin surface is also concentrated, so composability does not equal neutrality. cUSDO is a formatting layer over the same dollar claim, and in DeFi, formatting layers have a habit of becoming risk layers.

syusd-aegis.title: Aegis Cooldown Wrapper
syusd-aegis.text: sYUSD is Aegis's staking wrapper over YUSD, capitalizing funding-rate income into a rising exchange rate instead of paying out a separate coupon. The parent stablecoin risk is YUSD's BTC spot plus short-perpetual hedge model and off-exchange custody assumptions; the wrapper risk is the ERC-4626 vault, bridge footprint, and seven-day cooldown before holders get back to liquid YUSD. Accountable provides real-time reserve visibility, which is useful, but it does not turn a delta-neutral basis trade into a bank deposit. The product is different enough from YUSD to deserve its own row and similar enough that anyone pretending the risks are independent is doing spreadsheet theater.

stusds-sky.title: Sky Risk-Capital USDS
stusds-sky.text: Sky's expert-mode risk-capital module over USDS that funds SKY-backed borrowing and absorbs shortfall via slashing. stUSDS is Sky's expert-mode risk-capital token, not a plain sUSDS savings receipt. Deposited USDS funds SKY-backed borrowing while idle liquidity earns the Sky Savings Rate, exposing holders to borrower shortfall, governance slashing, utilization, and withdrawal-liquidity risk. As a {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} module distinct from passive {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} paths, it inherits the broad Sky/USDS ecosystem and ranks differently from USDS and sUSDS because its value can be affected by staked-SKY loan performance.

stcusd-cap.title: Cap Yield Wrapper
stcusd-cap.text:
Cap's ERC-4626 staked wrapper of cUSD where operators borrow reserves against restaker collateral and repay above hurdle — adding operator, restaker, and vault risk on top.

stcUSD is the {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} version of Cap cUSD. Users stake cUSD into an ERC-4626 vault while Cap operators borrow reserve assets against restaker collateral and repay with yield above the hurdle rate. Cap's design attempts to keep stablecoin holders whole through {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} and slashing, but stcUSD still adds operator, restaker, strategy, and vault risk on top of the underlying cUSD basket and its {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} mechanics.

said-gaib.title: AI Infrastructure NAV Token
said-gaib.text:
GAIB's staked AID vault token floats with the NAV of AI infrastructure financing positions — a different asset profile from AID's stable base.

sAID is GAIB's staked AID vault token. Unlike AID, which is intended as the stable base currency backed by {{term:treasury}}Treasuries{{/term}} and accepted stablecoins, sAID floats with the NAV of AI infrastructure financing positions plus stable reserve buffers — a {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} wrapper sitting on a private credit book. Monthly withdrawal cycles, unrealized-loss-aware unstaking NAV, and private AI financing exposure make it a materially different asset from AID.

msy-main-street.title: Main Street Strategy Share
msy-main-street.text: Yield share over msUSD that accrues from Main Street's options/derivatives strategy reserve; exit requires conversion back through msUSD, carrying strategy, custody, and liquidity risk on top of base USDC redemption. msY is Main Street's {{term:yield-bearing}}yield share{{/term}} over msUSD. It accrues value from the protocol's options and derivatives strategy reserve, while final exit ultimately depends on converting back through msUSD and Main Street's USDC {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} process. The token therefore carries strategy execution, exchange/{{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, liquidity, and governance risk separate from the base msUSD row.

yusd-yieldfi.title: YieldFi USDC Strategy Vault
yusd-yieldfi.text:
ERC-4626 USDC vault allocating across Pendle PTs, Morpho/Silo vaults, and private credit; risk is allocator decisions and venue performance, not USDC backing.

YieldFi yUSD is an ERC-4626 {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} vault over USDC that allocates capital across Pendle principal tokens, Morpho and Silo vaults, and private-credit vaults. Its stability depends on USDC as the native underlying, but its holder risk comes from active allocator decisions and the performance of those yield venues. Pharos tracks it separately from Aegis YUSD and YO Protocol yoUSD because the name collision hides a distinct issuer and reserve strategy.

sbold-k3-capital.title: K3 Stability Pool BOLD
sbold-k3-capital.text:
A K3-managed ERC-4626 wrapper around BOLD deployed into Liquity V2 Stability Pools — earning interest and liquidation gains but adding vault, oracle, and solver risk.

sBOLD is K3 Capital's ERC-4626 wrapper around BOLD deposited into Liquity V2 Stability Pools. It earns interest and {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} gains while automating the conversion of liquidated ETH and LST collateral back into BOLD. The base BOLD system is immutable and fully on-chain with {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-based issuance, but sBOLD adds K3-controlled vault, oracle, solver, and fee-switch risk, so it belongs as a separate wrapper exposure.

ybold-yearn.title: Yearn's BOLD Stability Pool Vault
ybold-yearn.text:
Yearn's ERC-4626 wrapper deploys BOLD into Liquity V2 Stability Pools, layering vault and strategy risk onto Liquity's CDP-redemption design.

yBOLD is Yearn's ERC-4626 wrapper around BOLD deposited into Liquity V2 Stability Pool strategies — a {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} wrapper that auto-compounds {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} rewards from Liquity's {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} system. It keeps the economic exposure anchored to BOLD while automating allocation across Stability Pools and liquidation-reward compounding through Yearn-managed strategy contracts. Holders can {{term:redemption}}redeem{{/term}} the vault share back into BOLD at the live exchange rate, but the exposure is not the same as holding base BOLD: it adds Yearn vault governance, strategy execution, auction, and smart-contract risk on top of Liquity's collateral-redemption design.

stkgho-umbrella-aave.title: Aave Umbrella GHO Staking
stkgho-umbrella-aave.text: Aave Umbrella stkGHO is a slashable staking receipt over GHO, which makes it much more interesting than a passive savings wrapper and much less comfortable to hold during a deficit event. Depositors earn Umbrella rewards, but they also accept cooldowns, withdrawal windows, and automated loss absorption if covered GHO shortfalls materialize. The wrapper minting is deposit accounting, while durable GHO issuance still inherits Aave's facilitator and governance controls underneath. Pharos therefore treats stkGHO as a risk-absorption asset, not a cleaner version of the base CDP stablecoin. A June restructuring sharpened the sorting: Aave auto-migrated passive legacy stakers into the non-slashable sGHO wrapper, leaving Umbrella stkGHO as the explicit opt-in vault for those paid to absorb losses. The yield is the payment for being useful when something goes wrong, which is a sentence no one should skip over.

myrc-blox.title: First Malaysian Ringgit stablecoin
myrc-blox.text: First Malaysian ringgit stablecoin, 1:1 MYR at Maybank under UTMB trustee with monthly attestations; eKYC-gated to Malaysian residents, unlicensed by BNM/SC, tiny supply, single-bank single-jurisdiction concentration. MYRC is a Malaysian Ringgit-pegged stablecoin issued by Blox Blockchain Sdn Bhd, deployed natively on Ethereum, Arbitrum, Base, and Solana. Each token is collateralised 1:1 by MYR cash deposits held at Maybank under the trustee {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} of Universal Trustee (Malaysia) Bhd. Mint and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} flow through Malaysian banking rails (FPX) and require eKYC via MyKad, restricting access to Malaysian residents with linked local bank accounts. Blox publishes monthly third-party {{term:attestation}}attestations{{/term}} on its transparency page, but the issuer holds no license from Bank Negara Malaysia or the Securities Commission Malaysia — SC Malaysia disclaimed jurisdiction in 2022 and BNM has not yet finalised a stablecoin framework. Circulating supply is small (~MYR 5.3M) and reserves are concentrated in a single bank and trustee in a single jurisdiction.

krwq-iq.title: First Korean Won stablecoin, RWA-backed
krwq-iq.text: First 1:1 KRW stablecoin from IQ/Frax, transitioning from USDC backing to a Korean T-bond-heavy reserve via Etherfuse Stablebonds; KYC-gated institutional access. KRWQ is the first stablecoin pegged 1:1 to the South Korean won, launched October 2025 by IQ in partnership with Frax. It uses LayerZero's Omnichain Fungible Token (OFT) standard with Ethereum as the canonical mint chain and Base as the primary bridged destination, sharing unified supply across deployments. Reserves are transitioning from initial USDC backing toward a target mix dominated by short-term Korean Treasury Bonds, which are tokenized through Etherfuse's Stablebond framework and held in segregated, bankruptcy-remote custody at Shinhan Securities, alongside USDC and Frax frxUSD. Mint and redemption are KYC-gated to institutional counterparties (exchanges, market makers, OTC desks), and KRWQ is explicitly not marketed to South Korean residents while domestic stablecoin legislation moves through the National Assembly. The transparency stack took a real step in June when KRWQ became the first Korean won stablecoin wired into Chainlink Proof of Reserve for automated verification, though the promised independent monthly attestations still lack a named auditor. Reserves anchor on tokenized Korean {{term:treasury}}treasury bonds{{/term}} as {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} held in segregated Shinhan Securities {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, with KYC-gated {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} and LayerZero OFT acting as the cross-chain {{term:bridge}}bridge{{/term}}.

reur-royal-euro.title: Euro Rail, Early Liquidity
reur-royal-euro.text:
A new euro-referenced stable from RIB Digital Holdings with meaningful early market cap but thinner reserve disclosure than mature euro peers.

REUR is a euro-referenced stable-value token issued by RIB Digital Holdings Limited and tracked by CoinGecko across Ethereum, BNB Chain, and Tron. The token has meaningful early market capitalization for a new euro peg, but reserve and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} disclosures are thinner than the larger euro issuers already covered by Pharos, so its risk profile depends heavily on issuer execution rather than mature public transparency.

kgst-kyrgyz-som.title: Central Asia's On-Chain Som
kgst-kyrgyz-som.text: Kyrgyz som stablecoin on BNB Chain claiming 1:1 KGS bank reserves; no verified attestation cadence, USD normalization via secondary FX feeds. KGST is a Kyrgyz som stablecoin tracked by CoinGecko on BNB Chain. It is presented as a fully backed 1:1 KGS token, giving Pharos a direct Central Asian local-currency peg, but public reserve and redemption materials remain limited compared with established regulated fiat issuers. KGST also depends on secondary FX feeds for USD normalization because CoinGecko does not currently expose a native KGS quote. Without a verified cadence of {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}, transparent {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, or a documented {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} window, the issuer's 1:1 claim remains unaudited by Pharos.

audx-aussie-dollar-token.title: AUD Liquidity With Sparse Footing
audx-aussie-dollar-token.text: AUDX is TAU Pty Ltd's centralized Australian dollar stablecoin, designed for 1:1 AUD {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} and backed by AUD cash and government-backed instruments. AUDX is an Australian dollar stablecoin issued by Tau Pty Ltd, trading as AUDX Token, and tracked by CoinGecko across Ethereum, Polygon, and Conflux. The issuer describes AUSTRAC registration and 1:1 AUD reserves held in regulated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} at financial institutions. Market depth is still small, so Pharos treats the reserve story as useful but less battle-tested than older AUD rails with longer public operating histories.

cngn-compliant-naira.title: Naira Settlement Goes Multichain
cngn-compliant-naira.text: cNGN is a Nigerian naira stablecoin that looks more like regulated settlement plumbing than a speculative dollar substitute. The reserve mix is split between commercial-bank naira deposits and naira money-market or short-term FGN treasury-bill exposure, with monthly independent attestations noted in Pharos metadata. Nigerian SEC oversight gives it a clearer regulatory anchor than most local-currency experiments, though that does not magically create deep secondary liquidity. The multichain footprint improves utility for payments and exchange settlement, while issuer-controlled Safes and a Solana mint key keep governance firmly centralized. The argument is starting to attract builders — HyperFX, a new on-chain FX engine, settles its naira leg in cNGN. cNGN's best argument is not crypto novelty; it is that compliant naira rails are useful precisely because everyone else keeps trying to dollarize the problem.

brl1-brl1.title: Small-Cap Real Exposure
brl1-brl1.text: BRL1 is a centralized Brazilian real stablecoin, targeting a 1:1 peg with a BRL reserve mix of Brazilian {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} ETFs, repo agreements, and cash equivalents. BRL1 is a Brazilian real stablecoin tracked by CoinGecko on Polygon. It adds another BRL-denominated route alongside the older Brazilian real tokens in Pharos, but with a smaller operating footprint and less public reserve transparency than the most established local issuers, including the absence of regular third-party {{term:attestation}}attestations{{/term}}. Pharos therefore models the peg as issuer-backed while keeping disclosure confidence conservative.

wars-argentine-peso.title: ARS Peg With Split Signals
wars-argentine-peso.text: WARS is an Argentine peso stablecoin from Ripio's wFIAT suite, tracked across six EVM chains with the same contract address but weaker reserve and redemption confidence than major fiat issuers. WARS is an Argentine peso stablecoin tracked by DefiLlama across Ethereum, Base, World Chain, BNB Chain, Polygon, and Gnosis, with CoinGecko also listing the token below the current $1M market-cap threshold. That split makes it eligible through DefiLlama coverage but still a higher-uncertainty addition: the same contract address appears across the EVM deployments via {{term:bridge}}bridge{{/term}} infrastructure, while ARS {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} confidence remain weaker than major fiat issuers.

pusd-polymarket.title: The Prediction-Market Wrapper
pusd-polymarket.text:
An application-tier dollar balance token mapped to USDC on Polygon, with risk concentrated in the Polymarket app rails rather than a new reserve.

Polymarket USD is the dollar balance token used around Polymarket deposits and withdrawals on Polygon. Its collateral story is simple: the token is intended to map to USDC and USDC.e in Polymarket rails, so reserve risk is mostly wrapper, {{term:bridge}}bridge{{/term}}, and app-access risk rather than a new asset mix. Pharos enables curated reserve validation against the Polygon contract and keeps the {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} path documented through Polymarket docs. Scale is the new fact: supply has blown past half a billion dollars on record prediction-market volume — an election cycle and a World Cup will do that — which makes the wrapper's app-rail risk a materially bigger number than it was in spring. The token functions as an application dollar, not an independent issuer reserve.

rusd-royal-dollar.title: The Royal Reserve Claim
rusd-royal-dollar.text:
A Royal/R Coins fiat-backed dollar on three chains whose reserve composition and redemption mechanics are not yet transparent enough to model rigorously.

Royal Dollar presents itself as a fiat-backed dollar issued by the Royal/R Coins ecosystem across Ethereum, BSC, and Tron. Public material supports the existence of issuer-managed reserves, but the composition and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} mechanics are not transparent enough to model as a high-quality fiat backstop. Pharos classifies the collateral as {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}}-backed while assigning a high reserve-risk slice until stronger {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} data exists. Reserve validation is limited to confirming tracked on-chain supply and displaying the curated reserve view.

usdr-ring.title: The Ring Protocol Dollar
usdr-ring.text: Ring Protocol's USDR is a small crypto-backed synthetic dollar with modest documentation; the dashboard models the reserve stack conservatively as protocol collateral and liquidity positions. Ring USD is a crypto-backed synthetic dollar from Ring Protocol. Its public footprint is small, so the dashboard models the reserve stack conservatively as protocol collateral and liquidity positions rather than a granular attested basket. The Ethereum supply is eligible for curated reserve validation, but {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} quality still depends on Ring-specific mechanics and protocol liquidity. That makes USDR a long-tail collateralized dollar with meaningful smart-contract and governance dependency.

uusd-anything-labs.title: The BSC Unity Dollar
uusd-anything-labs.text: Unity USD is a small BSC dollar token from Anything Labs with limited public reserve detail — tracked with a high-risk reserve slice and conservative redemption assumptions. Unity USD is a BSC dollar token from the UUSD/Anything Labs ecosystem. The collateral and peg design are presented as protocol managed via {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-style {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} mechanics, but public reserve detail is limited, so Pharos uses a single high-risk reserve slice rather than implying precision. The BSC contract is tracked for supply and curated reserve validation. Until clearer reserve proofs are available, UUSD remains a small, governance-dependent crypto-backed stablecoin where {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} parameters and exit liquidity are not externally verifiable.

jusd-jusd-stable-token.title: The Small Multichain Dollar
jusd-jusd-stable-token.text: Long-tail multichain USD token (BSC + Polygon) with issuer/protocol-managed crypto collateral; reserve composition unverified. JUSD is a long-tail dollar token with BSC and Polygon contracts and issuer/protocol documentation. Pharos models its reserves as protocol-managed crypto collateral because public materials do not provide a reviewed, granular collateral breakdown. The BSC deployment is used for curated validation, while Polygon is kept for discovery. Its main risk is not the stated dollar target, but the limited transparency around reserve composition and live redemption depth. Until JUSD publishes a third-party {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} and discloses {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, the {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop and reserve quality remain unmodelled by Pharos.

jusd-juicedollar.title: Bitcoin-backed dollar on Citrea
jusd-juicedollar.text: Citrea-native BTC-collateralized USD using a Frankencoin/d-EURO oracle-free CDP architecture; sub-$1M cap, early-network depth is the main risk. Juice Dollar is a Citrea-native USD stablecoin minted from BTC collateral in overcollateralized positions. The design follows the Frankencoin / d-EURO lineage: no external price oracle, no admin-key intervention path in the published docs, on-chain collateral positions, and liquidation mechanics instead of issuer custody. CoinGecko classifies JUSD as a Citrea ecosystem crypto-backed stablecoin, but current public market cap is still sub-$1M, so the main risk is early-network depth and liquidation-market maturity rather than off-chain reserve opacity. The model is a Frankencoin-style {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} with on-chain {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} and bidding-based {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} standing in for an external oracle.

usda-alpha-partner.title: The Alpha Partner Dollar
usda-alpha-partner.text: Alpha Partner USDA is a BSC-only dollar token with more ambition than disclosure, which is a familiar ratio in the long tail. The issuer describes protocol-managed collateral and liquidity reserves, but the metadata still has no credible reserve composition, no independent attestation, and no documented mint or redemption mechanics beyond a role-gated token contract. Pharos can validate the tracked on-chain supply and record the blacklistable, admin-heavy control surface; it cannot turn vague collateral language into a clean backstop. The FDIC-style marketing claims are especially unhelpful because stablecoin reserves do not become insured just by borrowing bank vocabulary. USDA belongs in coverage, but the confidence level should stay low until the issuer publishes something less ornamental.

xdai-gnosis.title: The Native Gnosis Dollar
xdai-gnosis.text:
Gnosis Chain's native gas token is an economic claim on bridged DAI, so its peg quality cascades from Maker/Sky and Gnosis bridge infrastructure.

xDAI is the native gas token of Gnosis Chain and is economically tied to DAI {{term:bridge}}bridged{{/term}} into the network. Unlike a normal ERC-20 stablecoin, its canonical supply is native-chain accounting, so Pharos lists the WXDAI wrapper as a traded contract rather than using it as the supply contract. The reserve view is a DAI {{term:bridge}}bridge{{/term}} dependency, making peg quality depend on Maker/Sky DAI — itself a {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-backed dollar — and Gnosis bridge infrastructure. It is more infrastructure dollar than issuer token.

usdx-kava.title: The Legacy Kava Debt Dollar
usdx-kava.text: Kava USDX is a legacy {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} debt token trading well below peg, kept in the catalog as a historical depeg case rather than a healthy par dollar. Kava USDX is the older Kava Mint {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} debt token backed by crypto collateral and {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} mechanics, sustained by {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} that has not been enough to defend the peg in practice. The asset remains visible in DefiLlama provider data, but its market price has spent extended periods below the dollar target, so Pharos flags it as a legacy depeg-risk entry. There is no supported canonical token contract to attach for reserve sync. Its tracking value is mostly historical and analytical: it shows how a live provider entry can coexist with a prior depeg narrative.

xtusd-xt.title: The XT Exchange Dollar
xtusd-xt.text:
XT.com's centralized dollar token has minimal public reserve disclosure; Pharos treats it as CEX-issued credit with very high transparency risk.

XTUSD is an exchange-issued dollar token associated with XT.com. The provider footprint is enough to admit it through CoinGecko, but its main chain is outside the configured Pharos chain set and public reserve detail is thin. Pharos treats the reserves as issuer-managed CEX assets under undisclosed {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} with very high transparency risk, and no holder-side {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop is modeled. That keeps the token visible without overstating its redemption or reserve quality.

hbd-hive.title: The Hive Conversion Dollar
hbd-hive.text: HBD is Hive's {{term:algorithmic}}algorithmic{{/term}} dollar redeemable on-chain for $1 of HIVE via witness-set conversion, with haircut rules when system debt exceeds thresholds. Hive Backed Dollar is a protocol-native dollar claim inside the Hive ecosystem. It targets $1 through HIVE conversion rules and witness-set savings parameters, not through cash or Treasury {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}. That makes the collateral base reflexive to the value and governance of Hive itself, especially under haircut conditions. Pharos classifies HBD as crypto-backed and decentralized while flagging that the {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop is protocol conversion capacity, not liquid off-chain reserves — a distinction the market is currently pricing, with the token trading several percent soft of the dollar on sparse venues while the stress gauge leans toward the alarm end.

jpyc-jpyc-v1.title: The Legacy JPYC Series
jpyc-jpyc-v1.text: Legacy prepaid-payment yen token series predating JPYC's funds-transfer-token migration; retained only for discovery and validation. JPY Coin v1 is the older JPYC token series, separate from the current JPYC deployment already tracked by Pharos. It is backed by yen-denominated reserve obligations and legacy redemption processes rather than the newer funds-transfer-token contracts. The Ethereum, Polygon, and Gnosis deployments are retained for discovery and reserve validation. Its main reason to track separately is migration clarity, because the old and current JPYC contracts are not interchangeable. The legacy prepaid {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} model and its narrower {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} processes are the reason v1 is not interchangeable with the current FSA-licensed JPYC contract.

nxusd-nereus.title: The Nereus CDP Dollar
nxusd-nereus.text: Small Avalanche CDP stablecoin minted by Nereus Finance against overcollateralized lending positions; transparent enough to track, risky enough to score conservatively, with a sustained soft-depeg pattern. NXUSD is a crypto-backed debt token minted through Nereus Finance on Avalanche via {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} mechanics. The reserve stack is modeled as {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} lending positions, which makes the peg dependent on collateral volatility, {{term:liquidation}}liquidations{{/term}}, and protocol governance. Pharos uses the Avalanche contract for curated reserve validation, but does not infer a liquid par {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} path from that alone. NXUSD fits the small CDP stablecoin pattern: transparent enough to track, risky enough to score conservatively.

wemix-dollar-wemix.title: The WEMIX Ecosystem Dollar
wemix-dollar-wemix.text: WEMIX Dollar is the WEMIX ecosystem's native dollar token, now mostly interesting as a case study in ecosystem stablecoins that never escaped their home chain. Pharos admits it through CoinGecko, but the primary WEMIX chain is outside the supported contract universe, so there is no live on-chain reserve validation from the dashboard's normal EVM/Solana tooling. The reserve description points to USDC and fiat assets, while mint authority remains owner-controlled on WEMIX-side infrastructure and the issuer has already signaled a wind-down toward USDC.e. That leaves WEMIX$ as an issuer-managed ecosystem unit, not a broadly composable dollar. The token may still have circulation, but its strategic arc is already written in the replacement plan.

suiusde-sui.title: The Sui Ethena Dollar
suiusde-sui.text: suiUSDe is Sui's Ethena-whitelabel synthetic dollar, which means it is not merely USDe with a new chain label slapped on top. The reserve logic inherits Ethena-style digital-asset collateral, delta-neutral hedging, basis-trade execution, off-exchange custody, and the operational dependency on exchanges and custodians that make the parent design work. The Sui-specific twist is deployment control: a single admin role holder also controls the package upgrade path, so chain-native does not mean governance-light. Pharos tracks the Sui contract and DefiLlama visibility while keeping reserve confidence conservative because live Sui reserve checks are not yet integrated. It is a synthetic-dollar export, and exports tend to carry the paperwork of the country they came from.

vcred-vcred.title: The Hemi Credit Dollar
vcred-vcred.text: vCRED is a Hemi-based credit stable asset with thin public reserve detail — protocol credit and crypto collateral, no verified fiat reserve. vCRED is a Hemi-based credit stable asset with limited public reserve granularity. Pharos adds the Hemi contract and treats the backing as protocol credit and crypto collateral via {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-style {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} rather than a verified fiat reserve. The curated reserve sync can validate supply on the configured EVM chain, but it cannot validate the off-chain or strategy quality behind the collateral. The result is a tracked but high-risk long-tail dollar where {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} parameters and redemption depth remain operationally opaque.

mai-qidao.title: The Multichain QiDao Dollar
mai-qidao.text: QiDao's long-running overcollateralized stablecoin minted against crypto vaults across multiple EVM chains; resilience depends on collateral quality, liquidations, and governance rather than an issuer balance sheet. MAI is the long-running QiDao overcollateralized stablecoin, minted against crypto vaults across multiple EVM deployments through {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} mechanics. Its resilience depends on collateral quality, bridge exposure, {{term:liquidation}}liquidations{{/term}}, and QiDao governance rather than an issuer balance sheet. Pharos tracks the major supported deployments and uses Polygon for curated reserve validation. The entry also preserves the MIMATIC provider identity while presenting the more familiar MAI name.

spusd-soulpeg.title: The SoulPeg Dollar
spusd-soulpeg.text:
A small BSC dollar wrapping a soul-bound sUSDC position via Venus lending; no Pharos-reviewed holder USDC exit path makes it protocol-dependent.

SoulPeg USD is a BSC dollar token with protocol-managed collateral and liquidity. Public docs support the basic peg and contract metadata but do not expose enough reserve detail for a granular basket, so Pharos therefore uses a high-risk curated reserve slice and validates the BSC supply path. Until {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} and reserve data become more transparent, spUSD remains a small protocol-dependent dollar rather than a high-confidence stablecoin.

inalpha-nest.title: The Nest Vault Share
inalpha-nest.text: NAV-priced dollar vault token holding private/structured credit with nTBILL and stablecoin buffers; not a par stablecoin. Nest Alpha Vault LP is included because providers classify it as a dollar-referenced asset, but its behavior is closer to a NAV share than a par stablecoin. The token can appreciate or drift with vault strategy performance, so Pharos marks it yield-bearing and NAV-style. Reserve validation checks the on-chain token, while the reserve slice remains the Nest Alpha strategy book. This is useful coverage, but direct comparisons with cash-backed dollars are misleading. The underlying mix is {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} credit with an nTBILL {{term:treasury}}T-bill{{/term}} buffer, so {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} depth depends on the vault's liquid stablecoin layer rather than direct par exit.

eusd-telcoin.title: The Telcoin Bank Dollar
eusd-telcoin.text: Telcoin eUSD is a bank-issued dollar token from Telcoin Digital Asset Bank, operating under Nebraska's digital-asset depository framework rather than the usual offshore issuer maze. That regulatory posture is stronger than most long-tail additions, but Pharos still keeps the reserve slice conservative because detailed public telemetry and published monthly attestations are not yet as mature as the charter story. The token spans Ethereum, Base, Polygon, and Solana, with issuer and multisig controls doing the minting work behind the scenes. Redemption is a KYC-gated banking-rail process, not a permissionless DeFi backstop, so the trust boundary is the bank. The charter started paying rent in June, when Telcoin launched the first U.S. regulated on-chain bank accounts tied natively to eUSD through its Wallet V5 — deposit banking and a stablecoin sharing one regulated container. eUSD is what happens when a stablecoin gets a bank charter before it gets market depth, and the bank part is no longer theoretical.

money-defi-money.title: The defi.money Stablecoin
money-defi-money.text: MONEY is defi.money's crypto-backed loan stablecoin, closer to a crvUSD-style CDP than to a fixed reserve wrapper with tidy bank statements. Users deposit approved collateral such as WBTC and ETH, borrow against market-specific risk parameters, and rely on conversion ranges and liquidations to keep the system solvent. Pharos treats the reserve as protocol-approved crypto loan collateral and validates it through curated on-chain checks, but the live collateral mix is still less transparent than the larger CDP systems it echoes. The mint path is user-collateralized, while market onboarding and debt ceilings remain under partially bounded admin control. It is a serious fork of a serious design, which still leaves plenty of room for governance knobs to matter.

fusd-freedom-dollar.title: The Zano Privacy Dollar
fusd-freedom-dollar.text: FUSD is a Zano privacy-chain dollar token with limited public reserve detail and no Pharos-supported chain {{term:bridge}}bridge{{/term}} — visibility only, low confidence. Freedom Dollar is a Zano ecosystem dollar asset admitted through CoinGecko. Its privacy-chain context and unsupported chain mean Pharos cannot attach a contract or run reserve sync today. The reserve model is therefore a high-risk single slice based on ecosystem collateral and documented peg intent. With no independent {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} or verifiable {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} disclosures, FUSD remains visible in the dashboard while confidence is kept appropriately low.

fusd-finchain.title: A Rebasing Bermuda Dollar
fusd-finchain.text: FinChain Dollar is a BMA-licensed, {{term:yield-bearing}}rebasing{{/term}} dollar backed by tokenized U.S. Treasury bill and money-market fund products. The token targets a fixed $1 value while balances rebase daily, so the yield shows up as more FUSD rather than a rising NAV. DefiLlama provides the runtime price and supply path, while FinChain's own reserve dashboard and docs describe Taikang, ChinaAMC, and BNY Mellon/Finloop reserve assets. The main caveats are issuer concentration, eligible-customer access, and reserve transparency that is still issuer-led rather than a deeply integrated independent feed.

zsd-zephyr-protocol.title: The Zephyr Privacy Dollar
zsd-zephyr-protocol.text:
A Djed-inspired algorithmic dollar on Zephyr's Monero-derived private chain, minted against volatile native ZEPH with reserve-ratio constraints.

Zephyr Stable Dollar is a protocol-native private-chain stablecoin admitted through CoinGecko plus Zephyr Scanner telemetry rather than a supported Pharos contract path. Its Djed-inspired {{term:algorithmic}}algorithmic{{/term}} design mints and redeems ZSD against ZEPH reserve collateral, with reserve-ratio constraints intended to preserve {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}}. Pharos sources ZSD supply and reserve ratio data from Zephyr's official API, but keeps the reserve slice high risk because the backing asset is volatile native ZEPH on an unsupported private chain.

zys-zephyr-protocol.title: The Zephyr Yield Share
zys-zephyr-protocol.text:
NAV-style yield-share wrapper over ZSD that inherits Zephyr's private-chain and ZEPH-collateral risk through its underlying reserve dependency.

Zephyr Yield Share is the NAV-style {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} wrapper for Zephyr's ZSD yield reserve, not the base stablecoin itself. ZYS supply, price, and APY come from Zephyr Scanner because CoinGecko and DefiLlama do not expose the wrapper as a market row. Pharos tracks it separately so yield is attributed to the actual yield-share token while base ZSD remains non-yield-bearing. The entry inherits Zephyr's private-chain and {{term:algorithmic}}algorithmic{{/term}} ZEPH-collateral risk through its ZSD reserve dependency.

iusd-indigo-protocol.title: The Cardano Synthetic Dollar
iusd-indigo-protocol.text: Cardano-native synthetic dollar minted from overcollateralized Cardano-asset CDPs; Cardano supply remains curated rather than live-verified. Indigo iUSD is a Cardano synthetic dollar minted against overcollateralized positions in Indigo Protocol. Its risk profile is a classic crypto-CDP profile: collateral volatility, liquidation execution, oracle quality, and governance all matter. Pharos stores the Cardano asset identifier and DefiLlama provider ID, but Cardano supply is not yet live-verified. The reserve view stays curated until a Cardano-capable verification path exists. Risk is dominated by classic {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} dynamics: collateral volatility against the {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} ratio and the maturity of the {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} venue on Cardano.

cdp-enosys.title: Flare's CDP Experiment
cdp-enosys.text: CDP is Enosys Loans' Flare-native dollar, minted against FXRP, wFLR, sFLR, and stXRP vaults priced by the Flare Time Series Oracle. The mechanism is a Liquity V2 friendly fork: user-set borrow rates, a Stability Pool for liquidations, and redemptions against the lowest-rate positions when the market stops pretending one CDP is worth one dollar. That is a more interesting peg engine than another issuer IOU, but it still concentrates risk in Flare collateral depth, oracle assumptions, and Enosys governance parameters. Pharos treats the mint path as bounded by overcollateralized vault rules, while noting that the token proxy and risk settings still sit behind multisig and proxy-admin control. In other words, it is decentralized enough to be mechanically legible, not decentralized enough to make admin risk disappear.

luausd-lumi-finance.title: The Lumi Floor-Dollar
luausd-lumi-finance.text: NAV-style dollar reference token on Arbitrum tied to LUA floor-price mechanics; not a 1:1 redeemable fiat stablecoin. Lumi Finance LUAUSD is not a conventional 1:1 redeemable dollar. It is a dollar-referenced synthetic tied to LUA floor-price and protocol-owned liquidity mechanics, so Pharos marks it as NAV-style and high risk. The Arbitrum contract enables curated validation, but the reserve slice is intentionally broad because public proof is weak. This entry is included for provider coverage, with a warning that the stability claim is nonstandard. The peg claim is closer to an {{term:algorithmic}}algorithmic{{/term}} floor-price reference than fiat backing, and no documented {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} window or third-party {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} is currently modelled by Pharos.

susd-solayer.title: The Solana T-Bill Rebase
susd-solayer.text: Solayer sUSD is a Solana Token-2022 interest-bearing dollar whose balances grow from T-bill exposure rather than staying as a static par token. The structure is simple on paper: Solayer workflows handle minting, the interest extension handles balance growth, and the reserve model points to U.S. T-bill or RWA partner exposure. The risk is in the operational wrapper, because holder exits depend on issuer workflows, Solana token semantics, and institutional custody assumptions rather than a permissionless redemption contract. Pharos uses the Solana mint for curated reserve validation and keeps the reserve slice conservative until a stronger transparency feed exists. The float, meanwhile, has drained roughly 85% inside a month with no public explanation — issuer-workflow exits working exactly as designed, in the direction issuers least like to advertise. It is a neat Solana-native yield wrapper, which is another way of saying the boring Treasury bill has acquired chain-specific footnotes.

usx-dforce.title: The Discounted dForce Dollar
usx-dforce.text: dForce USD is an older multichain {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-style stablecoin trading at a severe discount to the dollar, tracked as a depeg-risk reference rather than a healthy par dollar. dForce USD is an older multichain stablecoin with both stablecoin and {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} protocol routes, sustained by {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-style collateral and {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} mechanics. It remains active in DefiLlama, but current provider prices show a severe discount to the dollar target, so Pharos flags the depeg risk directly. The Ethereum contract is used for curated reserve validation, while the reserve slice stays broad because public collateral composition is not granular enough. USX is tracked, but not treated as a healthy par-dollar backstop.

home-homecoin.title: The Property-Lien Dollar
home-homecoin.text: USD stablecoin backed by U.S. home-loan liens and property receivables; foreclosure is the recovery path, not redemption liquidity. HomeCoin is backed by U.S. home loan liens and property-backed receivables rather than cash, T-bills, or crypto collateral. That makes the asset interesting but illiquid: a foreclosure right is not the same thing as immediate redemption liquidity. Pharos tracks the Ethereum contract, self-reported collateral source, and DefiLlama provider entry while assigning high reserve risk. The real-estate lending model is documented in metadata, but HOME is not classified as yield-bearing until a holder-level yield source is verified. Reserve risk is dominated by mortgage-lien {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} quality rather than cash {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}, and the {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} path runs through loan workouts, not an issuer window. The market has started pricing that structure honestly: the one thin pool where HOME trades currently marks it at a double-digit discount to par.

cdxusd-cod3x.title: The Facilitator-Minted Dollar
cdxusd-cod3x.text: cdxUSD is Cod3x's Base stablecoin minted by permissioned Facilitators against strategy-managed collateral; risk concentrates in those mint permissions. Cod3x USD is a Base stablecoin minted by protocol Facilitators under configured limits and strategies. The model can be powerful, but it also concentrates risk in facilitator permissions, collateral management, and strategy transparency. Pharos adds the Base contract and uses a single high-risk reserve slice until the backing is more granular. Its {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop is documented at the mechanism level, not scored as a liquid public route. Facilitator-managed minting resembles a permissioned {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} variant rather than a public {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}}.

susd-hedgecore.title: The Soul-Bound USDC Yield Token
susd-hedgecore.text: HedgeCore SUSD is a BSC yield wrapper minted from USDC and routed through Venus lending, with soul-bound behavior doing the opposite of what most stablecoin holders expect from a dollar token. The reserve dependency is explicit: USDC enters HedgeCore's strategy layer, earns through Venus, and gets reflected back through operator-mediated reward and exit mechanics. Pharos marks it yield-bearing but keeps the APY source conservative because a reliable public pool feed is not part of the current data path. The real warning is mobility, not collateral naming: early redemption is operator-controlled and the hUSDC wrapper only opens one direction. SUSD may be stable in accounting terms, but the exit door has a staff member standing in front of it.

usd3-reserve-protocol.title: The Reserve Basket Dollar
usd3-reserve-protocol.text: USD3 is a Reserve Protocol RToken/DTF that turns yield-bearing wrappers into a dollar basket, which is clever until you count the upstream assumptions. The backing is split across Savings USDS, Aave USDC, wrapped Compound USDCv3, and Steakhouse USDC strategy exposure, so holders are buying a governed portfolio of stablecoin yield rather than a single clean reserve. Reserve's real-time protocol feed and basket redemption mechanics make the structure more inspectable than most wrapper stacks. RSR stakers and governance absorb and manage losses, but that also means parameter choices and collateral onboarding matter as much as the assets themselves. USD3 is a tidy DeFi balance-sheet product; the sardonic bit is that its simplicity ends exactly where the basket begins.

sofid-sofi.title: The Fed's Own Stablecoin Customer
sofid-sofi.text: SoFiUSD is what happens when a nationally chartered U.S. bank decides the stablecoin wrapper is worth adding to old-fashioned cash at the Federal Reserve. The reserve model is pristine by crypto standards: cash or cash equivalents at SoFi Bank's Fed master account, independent audit coverage, and BitGo infrastructure for 1:1 mint and redemption. The control surface is still centralized, with BitGo-operated EOA roles on an upgradeable Ethereum contract, so this is bank-grade issuance rather than permissionless money. The interesting question is distribution, not solvency: SoFi can technically issue a credible stablecoin, but it still has to decide whether its retail users are meant to notice the token or simply see dollars. SOFID is boring in the reserve stack and fascinating in the product politics, which is a very bank-like outcome.

usdb-bridge.title: Stripe's Invisible Dollar
usdb-bridge.text: Bridge's USDB is Stripe's invisible stablecoin rail, with reserves at BlackRock {{term:money-market-fund}}MMFs{{/term}} under an OCC trust charter and distribution embedded in $1T of annual payment flow. USDB is the stablecoin most people will never know they're using. Bridge — Stripe's $1.1 billion acquisition — quietly powers Stablecoin Financial Accounts in 101 countries, turning every Stripe merchant into a potential stablecoin endpoint without the merchant ever touching a token. The OCC conditional national trust bank charter from February 2026 gives Bridge the federal regulatory cover that most stablecoin issuers spend years pursuing, and the reserves sit in cash and BlackRock money market funds with institutional {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}. What makes USDB strategically interesting isn't the token itself — it's that Stripe processes $1 trillion annually and can embed stablecoin settlement into existing payment flows without asking permission from anyone downstream. The competitive moat isn't technology or regulation; it's distribution through indifference.

hkdap-anchorpoint.title: Hong Kong's First Licensed Dollar
hkdap-anchorpoint.text: The first HKMA-licensed HKD stablecoin under the Stablecoins Ordinance; HKD-backed by HQLA in segregated accounts. HKDAP is what happens when Standard Chartered, Hong Kong's largest telco (HKT), and Animoca Brands form a joint venture to build the first stablecoin licensed under the HKMA's Stablecoins Ordinance — a regulatory framework that went from proposal to law faster than most jurisdictions manage a consultation paper. In May 2026 the project moved from paper to chain: Anchorpoint and OSL Group ran a full-lifecycle test on Ethereum mainnet — fiat funding, reserve, mint, transfer, and full redemption — without putting tokens into public circulation, which both advances HKDAP into testing and confirms Ethereum as the deployment chain. The HKD peg is backed by high-quality liquid assets in segregated accounts, regulatory-speak for 'we learned from Tether's early years.' The B2B2C model targeting RWA settlement and cross-border payments positions HKDAP as infrastructure for Hong Kong's push to become Asia's regulated digital asset hub, with a phased rollout still aimed at the end of Q2 2026. Whether the consortium structure — a bank, a telco, and a gaming company — can move at stablecoin speed rather than committee speed is the operational question, though a working mainnet mint-and-redeem cycle is a more convincing answer than most pre-launch issuers can show. The licensing playbook is built on segregated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, HKMA-mandated {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}, and a regulated {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} path scoped for HKD-denominated {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} settlement.

hkd-hsbc.title: PayMe Gets a Blockchain
hkd-hsbc.text: HSBC's HKMA-licensed HKD stablecoin (pre-launch, H2 2026) leveraging 3.3M PayMe users as its distribution moat. HSBC's HKD stablecoin is the second HKMA-licensed entry and the one with the distribution advantage that matters: 3.3 million PayMe users who already use the app for peer-to-peer payments and won't need to download anything new. The integration into HSBC's HK App for tokenized investment subscriptions hints at the actual product thesis — not a standalone stablecoin for DeFi, but a settlement layer for HSBC's own digital asset products. H2 2026 is the target, the reserves will be HKD-denominated high-quality liquid assets in segregated accounts per HKMA rules, and the symbol hasn't even been confirmed yet. The interesting tension: HSBC is building a stablecoin specifically to avoid depending on anyone else's stablecoin, which is either strategic autonomy or institutional NIH syndrome depending on your perspective. Expect institutional {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, HKMA-mandated {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}, and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} routed through PayMe and the HSBC HK app.

okrw-hashed.title: Korea Builds Its Own Chain
okrw-hashed.text: Pre-launch native KRW stablecoin of Maroo, Hashed Open Finance's sovereign L1 testnet built specifically for Korean Won; regulated and open issuance tracks, mainnet targeted for late 2026. Hashed Open Finance didn't just build a KRW stablecoin — it built an entire Layer 1 blockchain to host it. Maroo is positioned as the first 'sovereign L1' purpose-built for Korean Won stablecoins, with a dual-track design that offers both a regulated path (bank-backed, KYC-gated) and an open path (permissionless issuance). The testnet went live in May 2026 with OKRW as the native token, and mainnet is targeted before year-end. In a country where crypto trading volumes regularly rival the stock market but regulated stablecoin infrastructure is virtually nonexistent, the thesis is less about technology and more about regulatory positioning: whoever builds the compliant KRW on-ramp first captures a market that has been using USDT as a proxy currency by default.

arc-anq.title: The Rupee's On-Chain Debut
arc-anq.text: ARC is a pre-launch INR stablecoin from Anq, designed for a regulated 1:1 rupee peg backed by cash, fixed deposits, and Indian government securities. ARC is India's first attempt at a regulated rupee stablecoin, built by Anq with Polygon's backing and designed to prevent the USD liquidity outflow that India's regulators have been quietly panicking about since USDT volumes on Indian exchanges started dwarfing domestic payment rail throughput. The collateral — cash, fixed deposits, and Indian government securities — reads like a mutual fund prospectus, with {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} at regulated Indian banks, and the two-tier framework is explicitly designed to complement rather than compete with the RBI's digital rupee CBDC. The Uniswap v4 whitelisting for compliance is a novel technical approach to the 'permissioned token on a permissionless chain' problem, and primary {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} will run through KYC-gated issuer rails rather than open market making. Whether India's regulatory apparatus will actually let a private rupee stablecoin operate alongside its CBDC remains the existential question that no amount of technical architecture can answer.

brl-b3.title: The Stock Exchange Mints Money
brl-b3.text: BRL-B3 is a pre-launch Brazilian real settlement stablecoin from B3, Latin America's largest stock exchange, designed for its tokenized {{term:rwa}}real-world-asset{{/term}} trading platform. When Latin America's largest stock exchange decides it needs its own stablecoin for tokenized asset settlement, the signal is less about crypto adoption and more about what traditional financial infrastructure considers table stakes in 2026. B3's BRL stablecoin — branded B3RL — fills the gap left by Brazil's Drex CBDC narrowing its scope: the central bank's digital currency was meant to handle settlement, but as that project slowed, B3 decided to build the plumbing itself, backed by cash and government bonds inside its own clearing infrastructure. At its May 2026 Tokenization Day, OTC and digital-assets director Humberto Costa untangled the timeline earlier coverage had knotted together: the B3RL settlement stablecoin — built on Polygon — targets the first half of 2026, while the tokenized-share registry and B3's own tokenizer follow in the second half. The question was never whether B3 can issue a BRL stablecoin — it clears trillions annually — but whether Brazil's regulators will let a stock exchange run the settlement rails the central bank once reserved for itself, and whether 'first half of 2026' survives contact with the CVM.

usdf-flipcash.title: Coinbase's White-Label Dollar
usdf-flipcash.text: Flipcash's USDF is the first Coinbase Custom Stablecoin, a USDC wrapper used to prove out the stablecoin-as-a-service platform. USDF is the first stablecoin minted through Coinbase's Custom Stablecoins platform — a stablecoin-as-a-service product that lets any business launch a branded dollar backed 1:1 by USDC. Flipcash is the guinea pig, and the product itself is less interesting than the platform it proves out: if Custom Stablecoins works, every fintech, neobank, and loyalty program can have its own branded dollar without touching reserve management. The dependency chain is explicit — USDF is a wrapper around USDC, which is a wrapper around BlackRock-managed {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}} — and the governance is centralized-dependent because the token's existence depends on Coinbase continuing to operate the platform. Whether the world needs branded USDC wrappers or whether this is just a new distribution strategy for Circle's existing product is a question Coinbase would prefer you didn't ask too loudly.

krw-imbank.title: Quantum-Resistant Won
krw-imbank.text: Korean commercial-bank KRW PoC on Kaia with post-quantum security; symbolic of regulatory thaw rather than a commercial product. iM Bank's KRW stablecoin proof-of-concept has a feature that most stablecoins won't need for a decade but makes excellent press releases: quantum-resistant post-quantum cryptography via BTQ Technologies on the Kaia blockchain. Set aside the security theater angle, and the actual significance is that a Korean commercial bank is building a KRW stablecoin at all — South Korea's regulatory stance on private stablecoins has been cautious to the point of paralysis, and a bank-led PoC signals that the regulatory ice may be thawing. The Finger partnership handles the wallet and DeFi integration layer, while iM Bank brings the banking license and the KRW reserves. Whether this moves beyond proof-of-concept depends entirely on whether Korean regulators want to compete with Hashed's OKRW for the title of first regulated KRW stablecoin — or whether they'd prefer neither existed. As a bank-issued PoC, the stack assumes regulated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} of KRW reserves, statutory {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}, and a banking-rail {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} path that has yet to face commercial traffic.

gldy-streamex.title: The Yield-Bearing Gold Ounce
gldy-streamex.text: GLDY is Streamex's {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} tokenized gold ounce on Base, with Chainlink Proof of Reserve and gold-leasing receivables as the source of returns. Streamex GLDY tracks one troy ounce of gold while passing gold-leasing yield back to token holders. The entry is stronger than most new commodity tokens because it has a Chainlink proof-of-reserves feed on Base and a documented primary-market {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} route for eligible investors. The main caveat is that the yield comes from issuer-managed gold leasing rather than passive vault storage, so Pharos separates the live reserve feed from the not-yet-integrated APY source. Distribution is being built with unusual seriousness for a token this young — 24/7 secondary liquidity infrastructure with Orca, then a June brokerage-channel deal routing GLDY through Siebert's wealth-management desks with tZERO. GLDY is tracked as a commodity stablecoin, not as a generic RWA fund.

vnxau-vnx.title: The Liechtenstein Gram-Gold Token
vnxau-vnx.text: VNX Gold represents one gram of physical gold under Liechtenstein's regulated-issuer pattern, with AREVA reserve reports and Ethereum supply tracking. VNX Gold represents one gram of physical gold and fits the same regulated-issuer pattern as VNX's fiat stablecoins. AREVA reserve reports and {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}-style VNX documentation give enough backing detail to track the token, while the Ethereum supply probe provides lightweight live sync until a stronger public reserve API is available. Redemption is meaningful but operationally constrained: verified platform users can sell or request physical delivery from larger bar denominations. The risk is less the gold unit and more the issuer, custody, and platform access path.

xagm-matrixdock.title: Matrixdock's Silver Ounce
xagm-matrixdock.text:
Matrixdock extends the XAUm bullion-token model to LBMA silver, with issuer-reported ozPerToken drift the main reconciliation gap.

Matrixdock Silver brings the XAUm model to silver, with LBMA Good Delivery bars and public issuer pages showing supply and bullion metrics. Pharos uses one troy ounce as the silver reference, but the metadata flags Matrixdock's ozPerToken metric because the issuer can report slight dynamic drift.
